# The articles as graphs

Every article here has a semantic graph beside it: the ideas it rests on, the claims it makes, the methods and the examples, and how they connect. The map first, then one graph per article. Hover a node for its summary and an edge for its relation.

The graphs are data first and pictures second. Take them as JSON: [all articles in one file](graphs.json), with the topics, the teasers and the links between articles resolved, or one file per article at `articles/graphs/<slug>.json` (for example [this one](graphs/footprint-and-blast-radius.json)). The pages on this site are rendered from the same files at build time; nothing here is hand-written HTML. Since v0.7.77 each graph also carries the article's `figures`: file, URL, caption, the kind the author gave it (`wardley-map`, for one) and every frame of a multi-frame figure, so a picture and its context travel together and "every Wardley map on this site" is a filter, not a reading list.

262 of 262 articles have a graph. The map draws every article in date order round the circle, oldest at the top and clockwise from there, sized by how many other articles link to it. Teal edges run from an article to an earlier one it cites; amber edges run the other way, from an older article that was updated to point at a newer one. Thicker edges are articles that mention each other more than once.

## How the articles connect

*[diagram]*

262 articles, 1470 links between them (2220 mentions in all). 250 articles cite an earlier one; 72 links in amber run from an older article to a newer one, which means the older page was updated after the newer one existed. Most linked: [Fractal Semantic Graphs](#introducing-fractal-semantic-graphs) (40 articles link to it). Most linking: [A briefing for the WestCap CISO Summit](#a-briefing-for-the-ciso-summit) (20 links out). 2 articles not yet linked either way.

## [Application behaviour policies: what a website can reach, what it is for, and what it would cost if it were fully taken over, so the sites switched off for php2shell can come back with a known blast radius](application-behaviour-policies.md)

2026-10-22 · Agents & policyNews & evidence

A remote code execution flaw hands an application's whole reach to an attacker, so an application behaviour policy maps reach, mandate, gap, barriers and per-row blast radius with a way back, and decision and workflow policies say who accepts what remains and in what order, turning the decision to bring a precautionary-offline site back into a decision about known rows.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**12 nodes, 12 edges**

- **Agent Behaviour Policy** (concept) Reach, mandate, gap, barrier, footprint.
- **Application behaviour policy** (concept) The same words for an application.
- **Remote code execution** (claim) The visitor's grant becomes the reach.
- **Blast radius** (method) Per row, with a way back.
- **Decision and workflow policies** (method) Who accepts, and in what order.
- **Sites taken offline** (example) Councils, wikis, a cyber centre.
- **The bring-back question** (question) What if it is taken over anyway?
- **An invented council site** (example) Ten rows, five cheap cuts.
- **Our static sites** (example) The blast radius moved to the pipeline.
- **Signals** (method) The trace each open row leaves.
- **The compromise map** (artefact) 33 statements, as of 20:50 UTC.
- **No named compromise** (claim) Lower likelihood, same blast radius.

> An exploit is the moment somebody else starts using the difference. The method.

> A row the footprint never uses is a candidate to cut; a row used outside the mandate is a near miss. Reading the footprint.

## [A desk anyone can open: the PHP story's work and who did it, nine names with their responsibilities, and an evidence vault anyone can now read, scanned before its key was published](a-desk-anyone-can-open.md)

2026-10-22 · Vaults & methodSite & engineering

A story with many agent writers needs its work, its roles and its evidence written down where anyone can check them: a work file the build holds to its rules, roles drawn from the record, and an evidence vault opened with a read key only after a scan, read in the browser one source at a time.

*[diagram]*
**claim**method**artefact**example

**12 nodes, 11 edges**

- **Nine names, one chat** (example) The editor, three long-lived agents, an app builder and four collectors worked the story in a day.
- **The work as a file** (artefact) work.json: 24 rows, each with an owner, a status, times and proof.
- **Two rules the build keeps** (method) An owner must be a known name, and a finished row must name its proof.
- **Roles from the record** (artefact) What each name may and must not change, drawn from git logs and vault commits.
- **A name kept, not rewritten** (claim) The morning name stays in the history, with the reason, so the record can be checked.
- **The vault opened read-only** (artefact) A public read key that reads every file and cannot write.
- **The scan before the key** (method) 1,839 files searched for keys, tokens and personal data; none found, three things noted.
- **Public for good** (claim) A published read key cannot be withdrawn from anyone who has fetched the objects.
- **The browser that could not open it** (example) After four minutes and 742 requests the vault browser was still reading.
- **Read one source at a time** (method) The manifest in about three seconds, a source in about seven, screenshots on request.
- **A review for the story's site** (artefact) Ten changes ranked by impact, each against an article here, sent as a zip.
- **The move's five checks** (artefact) Read from the same file as the section, so the two cannot disagree.

> A history that changes its names when someone is renamed is a history nobody can check. Why the roles keep a retired name instead of rewriting the record.

> A published read key cannot be withdrawn from anyone who has fetched the objects, so before publishing it I scanned the whole vault, captures included The order that matters when opening a vault.

## [Capture first: how a BBC live page at breakfast became an evidence vault, a section here and a site of its own by lunchtime, for a story that was still changing as we covered it](capture-first.md)

2026-10-22 · Vaults & method

When a story is still breaking, the first thing to build is the vault that captures the evidence, dated and hashed, before the pages change, and the pages, the section and the dedicated site are then readers of that vault, with what went wrong kept in the record too.

*[diagram]*
**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**14 nodes, 15 edges**

- **The BBC live page** (example) Opened at 06:16 UTC on 22 October; a new post appeared between the first two copies.
- **Numbers that did not add up** (question) 70% of the internet beside 30 million websites, and agencies saying take sites offline.
- **Capture before you write** (claim) Live pages, down pages and posts change within hours, so the evidence is kept before the article is written.
- **The evidence vault** (artefact) A private sgit vault created at 08:03, holding 184 sources and 177 captures by 12:05.
- **The capture tool** (method) Raw page, rendered page, text, screenshot and headers, each hashed in a provenance file.
- **Captures are only added** (method) A page captured many times leaves a dated series that records how the story moved.
- **One file per writer** (method) A row per source and claims and timeline files per agent, so several agents write at once.
- **The /php-flaws/ section** (artefact) Pushed at 08:13 with what is known, what is not, the timeline and the claims by status.
- **NCSC-NL's inventory, bundled** (example) The whole repository kept as a git bundle; 674 products counted at commit cca173c64ec5.
- **Numbers pinned to measures** (claim) 70% of websites, 2.6 million hosts, about 6,000 resources in Latvia: different things measured.
- **Agencies disagree on offline** (claim) The NSA and CISA say take systems offline; the NCSC-NL does not advise it.
- **Forty sources nearly lost** (example) Two agents stopped before committing; the lead agent recovered their captures hours later.
- **A site of its own** (artefact) php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai reads the same vault, facts only, with briefings per role.
- **Retire the section** (method) The section moves to the dedicated site and leaves a pointer; the newsroom keeps context and opinion.

> A finished article can wait; the evidence for it cannot. The argument of the article in one line: why the vault came before the page.

> A count like 674 is only useful with the commit it was counted at, because the next pull request changes it. Provenance for a number, stated as a working rule.

## [The sidecar repository: a second repository the agent cannot write to, which checks every release against the policy, trusts signed checks instead of re-running them, and is the only thing that deploys, designed for an agent that is fully compromised](the-sidecar-repository.md)

2026-10-22 · Agents & policySite & engineering

A sidecar repository that no agent can write to holds the policy, a lock of approved hashes, private lists and keys, verifies GitHub's signed test results from the approved workflow instead of re-running them, waits for the owner when a gate changes, and is the only thing that deploys, so each attack by a fully compromised agent does nothing or stops the deploy.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**question

**9 nodes, 8 edges**

- **The sidecar repository** (concept) No agent can write to it.
- **The lock** (artefact) Approved hashes of every gate file.
- **Signed test results** (method) GitHub attestations for this commit.
- **Trust, not re-run** (claim) The 227-second tests run once.
- **Statuses ignored** (claim) Anything with a token can post one.
- **The owner's approval** (method) Only when a gate changes.
- **Private checks** (method) Lists the agent has never seen.
- **Total compromise** (question) What can a compromised agent do?
- **What remains** (claim) The owner, GitHub, valid bad content.

> did the deploy workflow, on this commit, produce this result? The question an attestation answers.

> Anything an agent can write, a compromised agent can rewrite. Why a second repository.

## [The rules of the game: a policy for which files an agent may change, and the least GitHub can enforce today without a new tool](the-rules-of-the-game.md)

2026-10-22 · Agents & policySite & engineering

Agents that can change the pipeline that checks them can pass any release, so the rules are written as a five-zone policy; on a public repository GitHub offers only a workflow-permission boundary for paths, so a hook and a CI guard make bypassing a deliberate two-step act, a token without workflow rights makes the guard a boundary, and a sidecar repository closes the rest.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**9 nodes, 8 edges**

- **Agents change the pipeline** (example) 62 of 227 commits touched the checks.
- **The rules of the game** (artefact) Five zones, from free to never.
- **Second key, not never** (claim) Agreement on changes to the checks.
- **GitHub on a public repository** (concept) Path rules only for private repositories.
- **A hook in the harness** (method) Catches mistakes; a setting.
- **A guard job in CI** (method) A second deliberate change to bypass.
- **A token without workflow rights** (method) Makes the guard a boundary.
- **The old-workflow gap** (question) An identical file on another branch.
- **The sidecar repository** (concept) Out of reach under full compromise.

> an agent may change content freely; it may change what checks its work only with a second key; it may never change its own rules The principle.

> An agent does not do both by accident. Two deliberate changes.

## [Where a check runs is part of the policy: tests as enforcers of Agent Behaviour Policies, and what moving them out of the agent's environment would gain, measured on this newsroom](where-a-check-runs.md)

2026-10-22 · Agents & policySite & engineering

Tests are deterministic enforcers of Agent Behaviour Policies, and where a test runs decides what kind of control it is: moving this site's checks from the agent's environment into a CI gate would take the deploy-blocking checks from 19 to 49 and, by estimate from measured parts, cut each release by about a third, but only if the new place is a gate, and only as boundaries once the platform protects the pipeline.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example

**9 nodes, 8 edges**

- **Tests as enforcers** (concept) Deterministic: run or not, pass or fail.
- **Where a check runs** (claim) Decides expectation, setting or boundary.
- **Today** (example) 19 gating, 26 on the agent's side.
- **Moved** (method) 49 gating, 7 with the agent.
- **About a third faster** (claim) An estimate from measured parts.
- **Only into a gate** (claim) 43 deploys after failed tests.
- **Platform protection** (method) Branch protection and reviews.
- **Signed test runs** (method) Skipping made visible.
- **Context-specific** (concept) Pipelines, not chat agents.

> Moving a check out of the agent's environment improves security only if the new place is a gate. The rule.

> A test is a behaviour policy in disguise. The idea.

## [Drift is the mandate moving: an analyst's case for policy and behavioural drift as RiskMandate's thesis, and why a versioned behaviour policy is what drift is measured against](drift-is-the-mandate-moving.md)

2026-10-21 · Agents & policy

Policy, behavioural, goal and authority drift can happen without an attack or a single broken rule, so detecting them needs a reference: a versioned Agent Behaviour Policy, against which a re-measured grant, every action's mandate row and every rule's barrier make three of the four drifts measurable now, as the Pellbridge demo's test pack shows, while goal drift remains the open problem.

*[diagram]*
**concept**method**artefact**example**question

**9 nodes, 8 edges**

- **The analyst's drift note** (artefact) Four drifts, a trajectory.
- **OpenAI agents weakened monitoring** (example) Legitimate tasks, controls weakened.
- **A versioned policy** (concept) What drift is measured against.
- **Policy drift** (method) The grant, re-measured.
- **Behavioural drift** (method) Every action against its row.
- **Authority drift** (method) What keeps every rule.
- **Goal drift** (question) The open problem.
- **Pellbridge's test pack** (example) Every model change, policy change, week.
- **This session** (example) Loses its policy, reads it back.

> Drift is the change nobody approved. The definition.

> without it, drift detection is anomaly detection with a new name The thesis.

## [A secret is a QR code and a link to a public key: the workflow the QR experiment opens, who else already does this, and a format to share](a-secret-is-a-qr-code.md)

Publishing a public key as a QR code and a link lets anyone, person or agent, return a secret encrypted to it as another QR code carrying their own key, so one exchange becomes a two-way, serverless channel trusted by a one-time fingerprint check; each piece is proven elsewhere, and the experiment's QRE1 frame can become a shared format with chunking, forward secrecy and an identity.

- **Agents in the loop** (example) Their own key pairs.
- **Prior art** (example) Certificates, key checks, device linking, wallets.
- **Signal device linking** (example) A public key out, a message encrypted back.
- **Quishing** (concept) QR codes as a phishing route.
- **QRE1** (artefact) One-line encrypted frame.
- **Three additions** (method) Chunking, forward secrecy, identity.

> It's just unusable. It's not practical. It looks messy. Why not text.

## [The Open Security Summit and its debt: how a summit that treated every participant as a presenter stalled on its own website, what the code shows, and why agents make it worth restarting](the-open-security-summit-and-its-debt.md)

2026-10-21 · Site & engineering

The Open Security Summit treated every participant as a presenter and its website was edited by its participants, but copying each year's site, adding exceptions and never refactoring froze the code, drove contributors away and left the follow-up unscaled; agents that map the data, personalise and follow up now make it worth restarting, in person, online and as a home for projects, if it is funded.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**11 nodes, 9 edges**

- **Every participant a presenter** (concept) Working sessions and outcomes.
- **The website as part of the summit** (example) 180 committers in 2018.
- **Copy last year's site** (method) 171 of 186 template files reused.
- **Templates grew** (example) 5,200 to 9,600 lines.
- **The code froze** (claim) No change from 2022; content kept coming.
- **The people went** (example) 180 to 14 committers.
- **Follow-up never scaled** (claim) No personal path per participant.
- **The material** (artefact) 409 sessions, 194 recordings.
- **Agents map and follow up** (method) Map, analyse, personalise.
- **The restart** (method) London, online, hosted projects.
- **Needs funding** (question) Someone to fund it.

## [Messaging-FS: an encrypted messenger between vaults, built on append lanes and PKI, from the first crude inbox to messages in the browser and on the command line](messaging-fs.md)

2026-10-21 · Vaults & method

Append lanes on every user's vault, combined with PKI, give an end-to-end encrypted messaging system between vaults, used from the web or the command line; Messaging-FS adds the schema, one JSON file per conversation beside Email-FS's one file per email, with each side writing only its own vault so there are no conflicts.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example

- **The first inbox** (example) Two agent teams, September 2026.
- **Rough edges** (claim) Tokens by hand, double encoding, partial signatures.
- **A vault per user** (concept) Billing or comms vault.
- **Append lanes** (artefact) Write-only, owner-read.
- **Four separated capabilities** (concept) Append token, enum key, write key, private key.
- **Encrypted and signed** (method) Lane, signature and sender agree.
- **Messaging-FS** (method) One JSON file per conversation.
- **Email-FS** (method) One file per email.
- **Each side writes its own vault** (claim) No conflicts; history is the vault's.
- **Web and command line** (method) sg.append; sgit pki plus a lane command.
- **The work list** (method) Derive lanes from keys, sign the whole envelope.
- **What it is not** (claim) Not a chat protocol, not anonymous.

> It worked, and it was crude. The first inbox.

> The client decides what the bytes mean. Why a schema is needed.

## [The user keeps the meter: a proposed design for user management, activity and billing on vaults, with one billing vault per user, two signed writers, and one light check at the server](the-user-keeps-the-meter.md)

2026-10-21 · Vaults & method

User management, activity and billing can move to the client: each user has a billing vault where their browser appends signed activity and adds credit as soon as they pay, while the admin side later checks payments with Stripe and commits signed validations, so the product keeps working on unvalidated credit and the one remaining server only checks a valid key and a cached signed credit.

**concept**claim**method**artefact**question

- **Pieces that exist** (artefact) Meter, append lanes, versioned vaults, key register.
- **The user keeps the meter** (claim) The browser appends its own activity to a vault.
- **One billing vault per user** (concept) Written by the user and the admin.
- **Activity and claims signed by the user** (method) Appended at intervals; credit added on payment.
- **Validations signed by the admin** (method) Verifiable by anyone.
- **Stripe read from the admin's browser** (method) List events; client_reference_id.
- **Three states of credit** (concept) Unvalidated, validated, not valid.
- **Credit now, validated later** (claim) The product keeps working; it costs nothing on the client.
- **Who are we defending against?** (question) Gaming the client: unlikely, easy to detect.
- **Pin the first commit** (method) Check every later commit; know who did what.
- **Upload server's light check** (method) Key valid, credit left.
- **user.sgit.ai or billing.sgit.ai** (question) So others can use it.

> A user very rarely runs several clients at the same time. Why the race mostly disappears.

> The product keeps working, and the credit simply moves from unvalidated to validated. Credit now, validated later.

## [A proposed roadmap for RiskMandate: policies, understand, risk acceptance, contain, manage and insure, a spectrum of trust we would walk with each customer](the-riskmandate-roadmap.md)

2026-10-20 · Startups & strategyAgents & policy

RiskMandate's proposed strategy, still being discussed, is a spectrum of trust walked with each customer, where each stage answers the customer's next question, from a single agent's policy through understanding exposure, accepting and containing risk and managing a fleet, to insurance, the end game that gives the path its arc; acceleration is the benefit of every stage.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method

**9 nodes, 8 edges**

- **A proposed spectrum of trust** (concept) Each stage earns the next.
- **Policies** (method) A microcosm; we are here.
- **Understand** (method) What is our exposure?
- **Risk acceptance** (method) Which risks, and who decides?
- **Contain** (method) A smaller blast radius.
- **Manage** (method) Agents run as a fleet.
- **Accelerate throughout** (claim) Not a stage: the benefit of every stage.
- **Insure: the end game** (method) Agents an insurer can cover.
- **Players at every stage** (concept) Partners, or an opening for us.

## [Can a key leak without breaking the policy? Told, checked, never given: three levels for secrets and personal data, and a hook we tested against nine leaks](a-leak-without-breaking-the-policy.md)

2026-10-20 · Agents & policy

Secrets and personal data leak as content inside mandated actions, so a behaviour policy needs content rows, and each is kept at one of three levels: told in the prompt, checked by a hook on every input and output, or never given, where something out of the agent's reach holds the key; a tested hook catches most leaks and misses encoded, split and piped ones.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example

**9 nodes, 10 edges**

- **A leak without breaking the policy?** (claim) Sending is allowed; the key is content.
- **Content rows** (concept) disclose.secret, disclose.personal_data.
- **Told** (concept) A sentence in the prompt.
- **Checked** (method) A hook on inputs, results and answers.
- **Never given** (method) The agent never holds the key.
- **Nine leaks tested** (example) Five caught, three missed.
- **Reading the key is excess grant** (claim) Use it, not read it.
- **Experimental rules** (method) Decode, match pieces, refuse base64.
- **3,451 real commands** (example) 22 refused, none ordinary work.

> It is the same action, with the wrong content. The answer.

> The three misses are not bugs in the first version of this hook. The limits of a check.

## [A small slice sets the price: what the 2026 mega-listings actually sold, how much of each company changed hands, and what founders should take from it](a-small-slice-sets-the-price.md)

2026-10-20 · Startups & strategyNews & evidence

The headline valuations of the 2026 AI and space giants are set by selling small slices, as the share of companies sold at listing has fallen for decades; the money raised is large, revenue is real but profit mostly is not, multiples sit near the dot-com peak, and the founder's lesson is that control decides the size and terms of the slice.

**concept**claim**method**example

- **Two numbers corrected** (claim) OpenAI has not listed; SpaceX sold about 4%.
- **The share sold keeps falling** (example) Median 30.5% in 1990, 14.5% in 2025.
- **The money is not small** (example) SpaceX $75bn, twice the previous record.
- **Against the market** (method) About a quarter more than Facebook's, as a share.
- **Record revenue, not yet profit** (example) OpenAI ~$50bn run-rate; losses and cash burn.
- **Dot-com multiples** (example) 28x, 20x, 57x against 31.7x and 38x.
- **A small slice sets the price** (concept) The last price times everything.
- **Arranged demand** (concept) Index funds must buy; low floats pop.
- **Control decides the slice** (claim) The founder's lesson.

> The headline valuation is the last price paid for a slice, multiplied by everything. The mechanism.

> A valuation is the price the market allows for the slice you choose to sell. The lesson.

## [Governs, enforces, attests: what an Agent Behaviour Policy does, the three levels at which its rules are kept, and why an attestation layer on top is the piece a third party needs](governs-enforces-attests.md)

2026-10-19 · Agents & policy

An Agent Behaviour Policy governs rather than enforces: it states each role's mandate and the level that keeps each rule, the prompt, hooks, or a recommended third-party blocking system such as Ruflo's policy engine, whose receipts an sgit vault keeps; an attestation layer that signs what was assured is the separate piece that lets a third party verify it.

*[diagram]*
**concept**method**artefact**example

**8 nodes, 7 edges**

- **An ABP governs** (concept) Reach, mandate, rules, and what keeps each rule.
- **Level 1: the prompt** (concept) Hope-based; the model keeps it or not.
- **Level 2: hooks** (concept) Deterministic, on the agent's machine.
- **Level 3: a third-party system** (method) Blocks out of the agent's reach; recommended.
- **Ruflo's policy engine** (example) Enforce mode, a decision receipt per action.
- **sgit vault** (artefact) Memory and receipts, encrypted and versioned.
- **Attestation** (concept) Signs what was assured for third parties.
- **Customer, auditor, insurer** (example) Checks a signature, not the operator's word.

> So an ABP governs. It does not, by itself, enforce. It names the enforcer. The precision the summary needed.

> a rule kept in the prompt should be attested as a prompt rule, not as a control What an honest attestation carries.

**concept**claim**method**example

- **Make it easy to pay** (method) Early, not at the end.
- **Do not worry about copying** (claim) It is all execution.
- **Atomic, changeable prices** (method) No subscriptions, no yearly contracts.

> Someone who pays more than it is worth, to help you, is not a market. Reading the signal.

## [How the newsletter is made: twenty-three articles, three issues, and every quote checked, written by the agent that makes it](how-the-newsletter-is-made.md)

2026-10-18 · Site & engineering

A newsletter issue is a narrative over six to eight articles built from articles read in full, where the build checks every quote word for word and the agent checks what no gate can, and the honest measure of the work is the backlog still waiting.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**13 nodes, 12 edges**

- **newsletter, in its own voice** (claim) The agent that writes the newsletter writes about its own work.
- **Issues 7, 8 and 9** (artefact) Twenty-three articles from 7 to 13 October, in three themes.
- **An issue is a narrative** (concept) Six to eight articles by theme, opening on a question, closing on grouped lists.
- **Plan approved first** (method) Dinis approved the themes on 13 October before any writing.
- **Read every article in full** (method) About 72,000 words, because quotes and claims come from the articles, not summaries.
- **Quotes checked word for word** (method) The build refuses a quote not in its article, or one whose paragraph does not link it.
- **The LinkedIn paste** (example) A quote's source line was dropped in the first paste, so the source moved to the paragraph above.
- **What no gate checks** (method) That each fact is in its article and no sentence claims more than the article does.
- **Overclaims softened** (example) "Never ran" became "did not run"; a removed hedge was put back.
- **The end of every issue** (artefact) The footer names newsroom.sgit.ai and the LinkedIn box names only the cover, since v0.12.25.
- **Rebuilt on top of others** (example) Two sessions released first, so the issues went out as v0.12.116.
- **Ninety-six waiting** (claim) Sixty-seven articles since 7 October are in an issue; ninety-six are not.
- **Propose before writing** (question) The grouping for the backlog goes to Dinis before the next issues are written.

> The order matters more than the speed. The plan and the reading come before the writing.

> What no script checks is whether my own sentences claim more than the articles do, so I read every draft for that. Where the agent's own check sits beside the build's.

## [A directory of people and their keys: pki.sgit.ai for the people I work with, verified by me first, then by each other, and a link that only counts when it goes both ways](a-directory-of-people-and-keys.md)

sgit has keys but no directory or web of trust, so pki.sgit.ai should register people: a passkey opens a vault holding their key pair, they publish the public half with evidence, Dinis verifies first, and links between people count only when both confirm in their own records, which stops the 2019 flooding attack; the point is to find someone and send them a secret by QR code.

**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**10 nodes, 8 edges**

- **Evidence** (method) Website, GitHub, DNS, other keys.
- **Dinis as the anchor** (concept) Verify, sign, the person confirms.
- **Two ways, or not at all** (claim) A link counts only when both confirm.
- **The 2019 flooding attack** (example) Anyone appended to anyone's key.
- **Degrees of separation** (artefact) Computed from confirmed links.
- **Invitations and secrets by QR code** (method) Scan, enrol, read in your vault.
- **Real keys in the register** (claim) The number to watch.

> A link exists only when both statements do. The rule.

> Being the anchor is a choice, and I would rather state it than hide it. On Dinis as the first verifier.

## [The editor's channel: what I read, sign off and want changed, sent to the newsroom's agent in a vault](the-editors-channel.md)

2026-10-18 · Vaults & methodAgents & policy

Editing from a chat loses the page, the version and the sentence; an editor key turns a browser into an editor's, which sends a subset of its reading to an editor vault, a daily pass acts on what is cheap to undo and replies, and five audiences each get a lane and a key, moving from shared secrets to key pairs.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**question

**12 nodes, 11 edges**

- **Editing in a chat** (question) Loses the page, the version and the phrase.
- **What already exists** (artefact) The pane, the lane, the inbox, append lanes.
- **The lane goes one way** (claim) Nothing comes back; nothing reads it unasked.
- **The editor key** (method) A key in a link fragment switches the mode.
- **The editor vault** (artefact) A subset of my reading account, newsroom pages only.
- **Signed off** (method) Against a version; stale when it changes.
- **The daily pass** (method) Checks, cheap fixes released, the rest proposed.
- **Cheap to undo** (concept) Articles are two-way doors; email is not.
- **Five audiences** (concept) From sending nothing to two-way.
- **The anonymous checkbox** (method) Append only: page, kind, phrase.
- **Key pairs** (method) Sign, seal, grant and revoke per person.
- **The brief** (artefact) For the agent that builds the pane.

2026-10-18 · Agents & policyVaults & method

The browser is the biggest attack surface we run and we now give it to agents; a minimal viable browser keeps a small kernel and loads components only when a page or agent needs them, boxes every extension, and gives each agent a browser with nothing to leak; Mozilla has the engine, brand and model to build it, and the pitch is speed.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example

**14 nodes, 12 edges**

- **The biggest program we run** (claim) Every feature on, for every job.
- **Bug counts rising** (example) 423 Firefox security bugs fixed in April 2026.
- **Less code already ships as a mode** (example) Edge without JIT, Vanadium, Lockdown Mode, Tor.
- **A small kernel** (concept) Network, TLS, parsing, layout, isolation.
- **Components on demand** (concept) Loaded per site, when needed.
- **Three shapes** (concept) One app, one agent, one reader.
- **A browser for one agent** (method) No accounts, extensions or files.
- **Prompt injection is not solved** (example) Vendors say so; PleaseFix was fixed by removing reach.
- **Every extension in its own box** (method) Only the sites and powers its job needs.
- **Trusted extensions that change** (example) ShadyPanda, Urban VPN, DarkSpectre.
- **Parts of this exist** (example) Forks, Brave Origin, Lightpanda, Tauri.
- **Why Mozilla** (claim) Own engine, privacy brand, client side.
- **Revenue is not independent** (claim) About 85% search, mostly Google.
- **Sell it as speed** (method) Starts at once, a fraction of the memory.

> An agent's browser that has no accounts, no extensions, no file access and only the origins its task needs cannot leak a password it never had or a file it cannot open. The agent argument.

> The pitch to Mozilla should not be security. The pitch.

**concept**claim**method**artefact**example

- **SECURE is the behaviour policy** (claim) Limits enforced outside the model.
- **VERIFY needs a definition of right** (claim) Someone must write down what right is.
- **The decision policy** (concept) Who decides the amount, on what evidence.
- **A gap in my own series** (example) The refund amount under the limit; a fifth state.
- **Three policies, four questions** (method) Every control in its cell.
- **The Northstar twin** (artefact) Thirteen cases, four designs, replayable.
- **Refusing is not being right** (claim) Design B leaves customers owed.
- **The wrong decider** (example) $261 in three refunds of $87.
- **Verification costs time until precedent** (claim) 57 minutes against 18.
- **A second model is not enough** (claim) Deterministic checks where rules exist.
- **The evidence for autonomy** (claim) The case record, and who signed it.

> So I would put his question to a team in two halves. Show me the cases. And show me who signed. The answer to his last question.

Once Dinis decided that a reader pays for what they read and not for what they scroll, the numbers had to be the reader's to correct: pause, reset and marks by hand; and once the newsroom knows what was read, it can step aside on a return visit or a scroll back up, in six views from a margin line to hidden, never while the reader reads forward, using a line and a paragraph written for every one of 1,897 sections.

**concept**claim**method**artefact**example

- **Charge for what is read** (claim) Dinis's decision: the meter charges for the share read, not the share scrolled; reading done on an earlier visit is not charged again.

- **The reader in control** (concept) The measure can be wrong both ways, so the reader can correct it.
- **Pause, kept** (method) Stops all measuring on every page until resumed, across reloads.
- **Reset and marks** (method) A page back to unread with a refund to the minimum; any section marked read or unread by hand.
- **Six views of what was read** (artefact) Full, Margin, Faded, Paragraph, Line and Hidden, chosen by the reader and kept in the browser.
- **Never while reading forward** (claim) The views switch on only on a return visit or a scroll back up, and a section on screen is never folded by the clock.
- **The words in view stay** (method) Before a fold the first visible element is noted, and the scroll is corrected after it.
- **A line and a paragraph per section** (artefact) 1,897 sections in 174 articles, each with about eight words and two or three sentences that say what it says.
- **Fourteen agents** (example) Each read a batch of articles and wrote their summaries; a script checked length, wording and coverage.
- **A summary knows it is stale** (method) Each carries a hash of its section; a corrected section marks its summary stale.
- **Summaries with every article** (concept) The authoring guide asks for summaries beside the graph, and the build counts extracts.

> Nothing on the page changes while you go down it. The rule that makes the views safe to switch on.

> A summary knows when it is out of date. Why a correction to an article cannot leave its summary lying.

**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

- **Binding precedent** (concept) Higher courts bind lower ones.
- **Distinguishing** (method) Facts differ in a way that matters.
- **Departing from precedent** (concept) The 1966 Practice Statement.
- **The loop for agents** (method) Rule, precedent, or escalate and record.
- **A decision record as a law report** (artefact) Facts, rule, decider, outcome, reasons.
- **Precedent to policy to code** (claim) A decision earns its way into code.
- **Delegation at the top of the agency scale** (example) Cases approved unchanged become rules.
- **Two cases from tonight** (example) A new rule, and a case distinguished.
- **Precedent can carry a bias** (question) Overruling matters more at volume.
- **No record, a self-report** (claim) The Ruflo run computes, writes nothing.

> Each step is earned by cases, not assumed in advance. The difference from writing every rule up front.

> Most agent systems keep a log of what happened; a precedent needs more: The record.

**concept**claim**method**example**question

- **Narrow, never widen** (claim) The scaling rule.

- **The tribunal fees case** (example) UNISON, 2017: unlawful from the start.
- **The envelope** (method) Money, blast radius, data, people, reversibility, duration.
- **The subset check** (method) Mechanical for numbers, flagged for words.
- **The VIP workflow** (example) 1,000 GBP against a 100 GBP limit.
- **Risk appetite** (concept) What the board is willing to take.
- **Kill switches at altitude** (claim) Where the envelope they protect is owned.
- **Envelopes can be gamed** (question) Split one refund into many.

> A lower level may narrow the level above it. It may never widen it. The rule.

> Each sign-off is small, because each level only has to read its own level. Why it scales.

**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

- **Data bound to its policy** (concept) The checkpoint records the rules in force.
- **Shown and inferred** (method) Solid arrows on screen, dashed inferred.

## [The policy guards the door; the command line uses the window: in the SGit × Ruflo run, the ABP is compiled into Ruflo's own rules and enforced on the adapter's tools, while Ruflo's command line reaches the same memory file without it, as the author's own README says](the-policy-guards-the-door.md)

2026-10-17 · Agents & policyVaults & method

Every step the ABP guarded behaved as written, but the policy is enforced by the adapter on its three tools, while Ruflo's command line writes and reads the same memory file directly in steps 3, 9 and 10; a policy holds only on the paths through its enforcer, and compiling the rows into Ruflo's own policy engine is one way to cover the rest.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**10 nodes, 8 edges**

- **Two paths to the memory** (concept) Through the gate, and around it.
- **The guarded steps behaved** (claim) 4, 5, 6, 8 and 11.
- **Ruflo's command line** (example) Steps 3, 9 and 10, no ABP check.
- **An agent with a shell** (question) Could it change memory unchecked?
- **A policy holds on its enforcer's paths** (claim) The general lesson.
- **This site's own agent** (example) Ten of eleven rules kept by the agent.
- **Outside the model is not enough** (claim) Around every path is the harder part.
- **Native plugin registration** (method) The author's follow-up: rules where Ruflo runs.
- **Five questions, answered in the code** (claim) Errors, records, the vault's home, a file name, approval.
- **The author documents the limit** (artefact) Only adapter tools pass through this gate.

> A policy holds on the paths that pass through its enforcer, and nowhere else. The lesson.

> Outside the model is necessary; around every path to the data is the harder part. The step beyond the conference.

## [Scrolled is not read: what the reading meter measures, what it should, highlights you can keep, and the page as the reader's own graph](scrolled-is-not-read.md)

2026-10-16 · Site & engineeringGraphs & knowledge

How far a reader scrolled is not how much they read, so the newsroom now keeps both, per section, in the reader's own browser: scrolled only grows, read is time on the words while the tab is in front and the reader present, counted against 300 words a minute; the page becomes a small graph the reader owns, with highlights anchored by quote, while the billing stays on scroll until the data says whether to settle it by reading.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**14 nodes, 14 edges**

- **The chip moves** (example) Dinis's two fixes: drop the balance the bar already shows, and stop the flicker; measured as 20 positions in 30 scroll steps.
- **Position is not progress** (claim) The chip showed where the window was, so scrolling back up made a page look unread.
- **Scrolled is not read** (claim) The meter charges by the deepest point scrolled and its foot block calls that read; a page flicked to the end is not read.
- **The reading meter** (artefact) A few pence a page from credit in the browser, charged by scroll depth in 5% steps, once a session, re-priced by the rating.
- **Engaged time** (concept) Chartbeat counts attention while the tab is in front and the reader acted in the last five seconds; Medium counts a read after thirty.
- **Reading pace** (concept) Adults read non-fiction at 238 words a minute, most between 175 and 300 (Brysbaert 2019).
- **Scrolled and read, per section** (method) Scrolled is how much of each section passed the reading band; read is attended time on it against its words at 300 a minute.
- **The page as you read it** (artefact) The chip opens the article as its sections, each with scrolled, read, time and highlights.
- **Highlights by quote** (method) Exact words with 32 characters either side, as the W3C annotation model anchors them, drawn with the CSS Custom Highlight API without changing the page.
- **The reader's own records** (concept) Everything is kept in the browser and sent nowhere; the vault is where it would travel, later.
- **Charge by scroll or by read** (question) Keep scroll, charge by read, or charge by scroll and settle by read when the reader leaves or rates.
- **Graphs are islands** (claim) 1,788 concept labels across 142 article graphs, only 32 shared: a shared vocabulary comes before more links.
- **Three prototypes** (artefact) Links: more, How this connects, and What you read, drawn from the newsroom's real data for the screenshots only.
- **Written by the agents** (artefact) A section for articles an agent writes under its own name, as briefs, kept off the front page's automatic lead.

> Position is not progress. The first fault of the chip, and the reason it now shows what the reader did, not where they are.

> Scrolling past is cheap. Attention is not. The one line from the research that the design rests on.

## [The fork next door: why open source protects founders, customers and investors from each other, why forks only take hold when someone stops executing, and why a maturing company should give its explorers a way out](the-fork-next-door.md)

2026-10-16 · Startups & strategy

In an open source company every corner of the triangle of founders, customers and investors has an exit that takes the technology with it, and each exit has a condition: founders need no broad non-compete, customers need their data to move, investors need to afford a team. Forking is a last resort and the famous forks that took hold followed a breakdown; where the original kept executing, the fork stayed a hedge. A maturing company can move a shared component to a neutral home and let its explorers carry on with the code.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example**question

**14 nodes, 13 edges**

- **The triangle** (concept) Founders, customers, investors; anyone can fork.
- **Forking is a last resort** (claim) 7 of 220 significant forks merged back.
- **Forks follow breakdowns** (claim) A new owner, a governance fight, a licence change.
- **LibreOffice** (example) 15,000 commits against 595 in 2019.
- **Valkey and OpenTofu** (example) Funded by companies whose businesses ran on the code.
- **io.js** (example) Forked, fixed the governance, merged back.
- **Execution is the defence** (claim) A rate, not a wall.
- **MySQL and MariaDB** (example) The fork stayed a hedge; MySQL commits fell two thirds.
- **No broad non-compete** (method) The founder's exit depends on the contract.
- **Nextcloud** (example) The founder forked his own company.
- **Data that moves** (method) The customer's real exit.
- **A neutral home** (method) Kubernetes moved to the CNCF.
- **Out-served with your own code** (question) Why Redis and Elastic relicensed.
- **Sell, don't issue** (concept) The fork as the investor's insurance.

> a competitor who forks today gets your position, not your velocity Why execution is the defence.

> So the founder's corner of the triangle is only as strong as the founder's contract. The condition on the founder's exit.

## [The controllable founder: why investors pick one founder over another who looks just as good, and what record labels taught us about who the commodity is](the-controllable-founder.md)

2026-10-16 · Startups & strategyNews & evidence

We study survivors, so the question is why one founder was chosen over another who did the same; the hypothesis is that investors select partly for control, moving the founder towards commodity as labels did to performers; investors prefer coachable founders though coachability does not reliably predict success, contracts hand control to investors when performance is poor and make leaving expensive, and half of founders were replaced by year three; founder control lowers valuations, but over the long run founder-led companies returned more, and the hypothesis can be tested.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**example**question

**11 nodes, 10 edges**

- **We study survivors** (concept) Denrell, 2003: undersampling of failure.
- **Investors select for control** (claim) One deciding factor between equal founders.
- **The founder as commodity** (concept) As labels did to performers.
- **Coachability** (example) Preferred, but does not reliably predict success.
- **Control in the contract** (example) Kaplan and Strömberg: control moves with performance.
- **Founders replaced** (example) Half gone as CEO by year three.
- **The investors' answer** (claim) Founder control lowers valuation 17 to 22% per level.
- **The long run** (example) Founder-led S&P 500 companies: 3.1x returns, 1990 to 2014.
- **The big stick** (concept) I leave and you cannot replace me; dual-class shares.
- **How to test it** (question) Follow the ratings; compare the mission; count the refusers.
- **Strong-minded founders** (claim) The profile the filter screens out.

> Coachability is a polite word for it. Controllability is a less polite one. The hypothesis in two sentences.

> Replaceability is not an accident of venture capital; it is designed in. What the contracts show.

## [Sell, don't issue: a funding model for founders who have already won, where the investor buys the founder's shares, the founder lends the company what it needs, and open source keeps everyone honest](sell-dont-issue.md)

2026-10-16 · Startups & strategy

A founder with a working, profitable product and competing investors can sell existing shares instead of issuing new ones, so the founder is paid and no control changes hands, then lend part of the proceeds back as a subordinated loan; open source replaces control rights as the investor's protection, because a fork gets the position but not the velocity; the costs are real: no EIS on bought shares, a signalling problem, a creditor conflict, and tax and articles fine print.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**question

**12 nodes, 11 edges**

- **Start from strength** (claim) Profit, growth, competing investors.
- **Sell, don't issue** (method) The investor buys the founder's ordinary shares.
- **Lend, don't dilute** (method) A subordinated founder loan, repaid from success.
- **The fork as insurance** (concept) Position, not velocity.
- **The same £2m, two ways** (artefact) 80% either way; who holds cash and control changes.
- **Why it raises the odds** (claim) Money discipline, focus, direction.
- **No EIS on bought shares** (question) Relief only on newly issued shares.
- **It can read as doubt** (question) Balderton: 10% at growth stage.
- **Founder as creditor** (question) Subordinate the loan by contract.
- **The fine print** (question) Transfer rights, above-market sales, results-linked interest.
- **Refuse a broad non-compete** (question) It keeps the fork for the investors only.
- **The controllable founder** (concept) The deal this is designed against.

> So the investor's protection moves from the contract to the commons. The core move.

> the fork disciplines the founder because it is possible, and protects the founder because it is slow. Why the fork balances.

## [Research, delivered as a vault: what companies that sell research could do with fractal graphs, behaviour policies for AI-enabled products, and evaluations run by a governed agent hive](research-delivered-as-a-vault.md)

2026-10-16 · Vaults & methodStartups & strategy

Research is sold by subscription and delivered as documents, one reading for everyone; delivered as an sgit vault it becomes findings with evidence, a fractal graph instead of one taxonomy, a briefing per reader, calculations, a branded app and an append lane back, refreshed as commits; for AI-enabled products the research should include an Agent Behaviour Policy with and without the AI, over which the firm judges licence to operate and insurability; the evidence can come from a governed agent hive with a ledger, and the whole can be sold by the block.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example

## [sgit is a standard, not a server: everything in a vault is one hash away, any storage can serve it, and the server is the least interesting part](sgit-is-a-standard.md)

2026-10-16 · Vaults & methodSite & engineering

Like git, sgit is a format rather than a product: encrypted blobs, trees, commits and refs laid out by a convention, immutable objects named by the hash of their ciphertext and marked -imm-, every name derived from the key so a file is four GETs from any host, writes one batch and a compare-and-swap, two implementations that agree; deployment is choosing where the objects live and speed is how close they are; a cache layer computed by the writer replaces server-side derived data; and the design is what remains when the server cannot read.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example

**10 nodes, 9 edges**

- **Git is a standard** (concept) Why it outlived every central server.
- **A vault is a convention** (concept) Blobs, trees, commits, refs; all ciphertext.
- **The name says -imm-** (method) Anyone can keep the object for ever.
- **Everything from one hash** (claim) The key gives every name; four GETs to a file.
- **Two implementations** (example) The CLI and the browser app agree.
- **Any storage reads it** (claim) Bucket, CDN, GitHub Pages, a folder.
- **Writes need one CAS** (method) The API's main job.
- **A cache you can compute** (artefact) sgit cache add; one batch read.
- **Merges stay on the client** (claim) A merge is a workflow step.
- **The constraint designed it** (concept) A server that cannot read.

> There is a server, and it is the least interesting part. The thesis.

> "How fast is sgit" is the wrong question. The right one is where the storage is, and how close. Deployment as storage.

## [One vault, ten agents, 35,000 objects: what sgit does when the repository is big and the clients are many, measured on the vault behind this newsroom](one-vault-ten-agents.md)

2026-10-16 · Vaults & methodSite & engineering

The vault the newsroom's ten agents share, 1,295 commits, 5,281 files and 35,000 encrypted objects, is the size of a real application's source repository; a full clone takes three and a half minutes but an agent takes one folder with one commit in 13 seconds and 3 MB, a file on demand in under 3, a pull in 2.5; without a depth a partial clone walks history one request per commit, a fix is designed; and from local disk the same clone is 0.8 seconds, so the time is the storage, which makes sgit plausible for source code.

*[diagram]*
**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**10 nodes, 9 edges**

- **The newsroom's vault** (artefact) 1,295 commits, 5,281 files, 35,000 objects.
- **The size of real source code** (claim) Like the SG/Send repository: 5,584 files.
- **A full clone** (example) 3½ minutes, 527 MB; nobody needs one.
- **One folder, one commit** (method) 13 seconds, 3 MB, whatever the size.
- **History walked per commit** (question) 227 s for a folder's full history.
- **A commit-chain object** (method) Designed fix: 26 batched requests.
- **The pull, fixed** (example) About 53 minutes to about 3.
- **The time is the storage** (claim) 0.8 s from a local server.
- **Many clients** (example) Ten scoped clones at once: 1.9 s.
- **A code base in a vault** (question) The next test.

> A clone that carries a depth costs seconds and megabytes however large the vault is The agent pattern.

> So sgit is not the bottleneck; the distance to the storage is. Where the time goes.

## [The value of constraints: what client-side encryption and open source actually gave us, which is not what you would think](the-value-of-constraints.md)

2026-10-16 · Vaults & methodStartups & strategy

Client-side encryption and open source are constraints whose main value is not the obvious one: encryption moves protection from the data to the keys and the sovereignty line to whoever holds them, without removing GDPR, but above all it removes the temptation to process on the server, so there is no server code and features like scoped clones follow; open source removes the temptations of lock-in, the evaluation edition and building every customer's integration, which is why it has to be all of it, and leaves selling customisation as the business model.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**12 nodes, 11 edges**

- **Encryption is not the selling point** (claim) Better features and workflows are.
- **Constraints drive innovation** (concept) An inverted U: some helps, too much hurts.
- **From the data to the keys** (concept) Protect the keys, not every copy of the data.
- **Sovereignty is who holds the keys** (claim) The EDPB treats it as an effective measure.
- **Not out of GDPR** (question) Still personal data for the key holder; Art. 34(3)(a) helps.
- **Nothing on the server** (claim) No temptation to process; no server code.
- **clone --path and static reads** (artefact) Features born of the constraint.
- **Open source as a constraint** (concept) No private code; easy to deploy and change.
- **No lock-in, no curse** (claim) Here is the code: integrate it, or pay for it.
- **All of it, or an evaluation version** (claim) Open core brings the dependencies back.
- **Relicensing produced forks** (example) OpenSearch, OpenTofu, Valkey.
- **Sell customisation** (method) The model left when the bad ones are removed.

> But I do not think anyone will buy sgit because it is encrypted. The mistake, named.

> once nothing can run on the server, there is no server code The biggest gain.

## [Software vendors should become villagers and town planners: let users explore on top of the product, sell them the maintenance of what they build, and use Firefox as the example of what happens if you don't](software-vendors-as-villagers.md)

2026-10-16 · Startups & strategyAgents & policy

When users can rebuild the 10% of a product they need, every friction becomes a decision, and what stops them is maintaining what they built; a software company should position itself, in Wardley's terms, as the villager and town planner under its users, letting them explore on top of the product by talking to it and selling them the maintenance of their versions, from a pound to a maintained fork; Firefox, a good browser funded about 73% by royalties from mostly one customer, is the example of a product that could take that money instead.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**12 nodes, 11 edges**

- **Every friction is a decision** (claim) Users know they could rebuild the part they need.
- **The signs are here** (example) February's sell-off; Adobe's apps cloned in the open.
- **What stops me is maintenance** (claim) Building it is cheap; keeping it working is not.
- **Explorers, villagers, town planners** (concept) Wardley's three kinds of people, as a product strategy.
- **Vendor as villager and town planner** (method) Users explore on top; the vendor maintains and industrialises.
- **Innovate on a commodity** (concept) Wardley's ILC: let the ecosystem innovate, spot what works.
- **Malleable software** (concept) Ink & Switch, June 2025: code generation alone is not enough.
- **Explore, keep, adopt, own** (artefact) From a pound a month to a maintained fork.
- **Firefox, a browser I could not bend** (example) Compact mode back in 157; no hidden toolbar on iPad.
- **73% royalties** (example) Mozilla 2024: $680M revenue, 86% of contract revenue from one customer.
- **Settings are not the answer** (claim) Primitives and design systems make variation cheap.
- **Who will make the move?** (question) No vendor found doing it yet.

> It is easy to rebuild 10% of a product's features. Why every friction is now a decision.

> Firefox is a good browser that I could not bend. The example in one line.

## [A custom Firefox of my own: the full plan to build one with a governed agent hive, for the laptop and the iPad, and how Mozilla could sell me the part I do not want to do, which is keeping it working](a-custom-firefox-of-my-own.md)

2026-10-16 · Agents & policyStartups & strategy

A custom Firefox can be built with a Ruflo hive, an sgit vault and a behaviour policy by putting each want on the least invasive layer, policies, preferences, the browser's stylesheet and an extension, and only the rest in a renamed front-end patch set; the iPad needs a fork of the separate WebKit codebase; with releases every two weeks the real cost is maintenance on two codebases, which is what Mozilla, already selling a branded build and custom development to organisations, should sell to one person, per release or per change.

*[diagram]*
**method**artefact**example**question

**11 nodes, 10 edges**

- **A Firefox that stays mine** (question) Laptop and iPad, next month and next year.
- **Hive, memory, mandate** (method) Ruflo workers, an sgit vault, a behaviour policy.
- **The brief and its triage** (artefact) Each want to the lowest layer.
- **Policies, prefs, CSS, extension** (method) Most wants stop before a fork.
- **A renamed patch set** (method) Front end, artifact builds; trademark rule.
- **The iPad is a second codebase** (example) WebKit, Swift, a developer account.
- **Every two weeks** (example) Since Firefox 155: 26 releases a year.
- **The maintenance loop** (method) Rebase, rebuild, test, report, approve.
- **Agents can carry patches** (example) PortGPT: 89.15% on 1,815 cases; people still check.
- **Firefox Enterprise** (example) A branded build and custom development, for organisations.
- **Explore, keep, adopt, own** (artefact) Free, 50p a release, £50 to £500 a change, a contract.

> After that, I do not want it to break. The whole point.

> you may not distribute a modified form of Firefox and continue to call it Firefox Why only Mozilla can ship it branded.

## [Scion and sgit: Anthropic rebuilt source control for agents inside one company, and an open-source encrypted version already does much of the same thing outside it](scion-and-sgit.md)

2026-10-16 · Vaults & methodSite & engineering

Agents broke Git's offline, full-clone assumptions at Anthropic, which built Scion: a server that does history, blame, merges and commits, immutable objects served from cache tiers, and clients that fetch only what they need; sgit reaches the same properties from the opposite design, a dumb server that stores encrypted objects named by their ciphertext, reads from any static host and objects any cache can keep, and scoped, shallow and on-demand clones, measured on the 35,000-object vault the newsroom's agents share; Scion is ahead on server-side history, merge, blame and proven scale, but it is internal, while sgit is open source and encrypts everything.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**11 nodes, 12 edges**

- **Agents broke Git's assumptions** (claim) 30,000 merges a day; always-online clients.
- **Scion: the server does the work** (artefact) History, blame, merges server-side; cache tiers; no full copy.
- **sgit: a dumb, blind server** (artefact) Client encrypts, merges and verifies; server stores ciphertext.
- **Immutable ids that cache** (concept) SHA-256 of the ciphertext; the name says -imm-, so anyone can keep them.
- **Fetch only what you need** (method) --path, --depth, --sparse.
- **Reads from any GET host** (method) --transport static; no sgit server in the path.
- **Compare-and-swap refs** (concept) Both move refs atomically.
- **Measured on a busy vault** (example) 35,000 objects: one folder, one commit, 13 s; the 59 s was a bug.
- **Where Scion is ahead** (question) Server-side blame and bisect; proven scale; history walked per commit.
- **Git side by side** (concept) Coexist in a folder; no history bridge.
- **Internal versus open** (claim) Scion unreleased; sgit on PyPI today.

> was actively undermining our ability to scale Anthropic on Git's offline, full-clone design.

> by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use Scion's own status.

## [Your agent's logs are a self-report: an answer to a GRC adviser's post on The AI Conference, with this site's own agent as the worked example, including the two commits its own counter got wrong](your-agents-logs-are-a-self-report.md)

2026-10-16 · Agents & policyNews & evidence

An agent's own account is a self-report, and research shows models rarely admit reward hacks; evidence comes from four sources of increasing independence, and this site's agent, measured against them, keeps ten of eleven rules itself, has one real boundary its policy does not list, and a hook-written counter that is more honest than the agent and still flagged two commits wrongly; owners belong to mandates, controls need testing, and the policy should be published.

*[diagram]*

## [The vault, opened: merging devices, reading every call to the vault server, browsing your vaults, and one viewer that every reader vault links and opens with](the-vault-opened.md)

2026-10-16 · Vaults & methodSite & engineering

The reader's vault became something a reader can see into and tidy: devices merge without losing a record, each call to the vault server is named and decrypted with keys the page already holds, a page walks every vault file by file and commit by commit, and one viewer, living in a vault of its own, is linked read-only into every reader vault as its app, the vault-in-vault technique proven in the live SG/App on a demo vault.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**13 nodes, 13 edges**

- **Five asks after Firefox** (example) Dinis connected Firefox, found the workflow worked, and asked for merging, browsing, a shared viewer, readable calls and a clearer chooser.
- **Merge devices** (method) Several device files become one, every record re-filed and combined, the totals unchanged.
- **Aliases, not deletions** (concept) activity/aliases.json sends a merged device's browser, files and inbox batches to the device it went into.
- **No payment lost** (claim) A top-up is a payment record; a merge moves it and never drops it.
- **A chooser that names the destination** (artefact) The likely device first, a button that says where the browser goes, and Change to move it later.
- **The Calls tab** (artefact) Every call named from its address, and opened into a commit, tree, ref or file with the vault's own key.
- **Your vaults, opened** (artefact) A page that opens the four vaults of an account and shows files, contents and commits, writing nothing.
- **sgit.ai's sub-vaults** (concept) A link file with no key, the read key in an owner record, and app reads spliced through the link.
- **Four files in the reader vault** (method) The link, the owner record, the app manifest and a short entry page, written on the next Update.
- **One shared viewer** (artefact) The viewer lives once, in vault lkypj6zq, and every reader vault that links it shows its new versions.
- **Proven in the live SG/App** (example) A demo reader vault linked the same way opened read-only and rendered through the viewer.
- **Only a read key leaves** (claim) The SG/Vault app is handed the reader vault's read key over its embed protocol, and the test checks it is nothing else.
- **Undo and deep links** (question) Splitting a merged device and opening the app straight onto its history are not built.

> Merging keeps every record and every payment, moves them into one device file, and leaves an alias so a browser still using a merged device lands in the right place. the rule of a merge, and the reason it is safe for money

> The viewer's code lives once. the whole of the vault-in-vault technique in five words

## [When journalism becomes intelligence, built: an observation desk for one data-center buildout, from an atlas of 78 events to a community impact tracker, in a vault you can open](journalism-becomes-intelligence.md)

2026-10-15 · News & evidenceVaults & method

Francesco Marconi argues that journalism's advantage moves to how it observes: delta science, an atlas of events with definitions and observable signals, a domain ontology and a persistent record of observations backed by evidence; built here as a vault app that follows his eleven slides on a synthetic data-center buildout, it shows that comparing each new record with the last is where the stories appear, that AI makes observing and comparing cheap while journalists keep the definitions, the checks and the judgement, and that a vault suits an observation desk because the history is versioned, the evidence travels with each claim and the read key opens it.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**13 nodes, 12 edges**

- **The advantage is how you observe** (claim) Marconi: as production gets easy, observation is the edge.
- **Journalism is delta science** (concept) What changed, why it matters, who is affected.
- **An atlas of 78 event types** (artefact) 12 families; each event with a definition and a signal.
- **A domain ontology** (artefact) Six entities, six relationships.
- **17 observations** (artefact) Subject, change, time, evidence.
- **Observe, compare, check, report, update** (method) One cycle stepped through in the vault.
- **What comparison found** (example) Permit grew, jobs shrank, schedule slipped, water open.
- **Community impact tracker** (artefact) Jobs, water, power, land, commitments; an article and alerts.
- **Where AI fits** (claim) Cheap observing and comparing; people define, check and judge.
- **Synthetic on purpose** (method) A fictional twin of the deck's real example.
- **Why a vault** (concept) Versioned history, evidence beside claims, a read key.
- **Make one for your beat** (question) Choose a question, map the system, define events, keep observing.
- **Five graphs of one knowledge** (artefact) Fractal, radial, knowledge graph in time, evidence, delta chain.

> As AI makes content production easier, journalism's competitive advantage will increasingly come from how we observe the world. Marconi's argument.

> not a pile of articles, but a graph whose every edge has a date and a source What a newsroom's memory should look like.

2026-10-15 · Startups & strategyNews & evidence

For twenty years the winning startup was often a clever outsider who found a pain point, raised on belief, hired the experts and displaced the incumbents, then became one; generative AI makes execution cheap enough that subject-matter experts can build the product themselves, which the data on founder age and industry experience always favoured; and Europe's investors, who want to see it working, value lower and fund later, suit a founder who can now build first, because money too early is one of the most reliable ways to kill a startup.

- **Disruptors become incumbents** (claim) Innovation fades; tools pile up; 83 security tools on average.

secrets.sgit.ai, a site whose app was never built but whose design already shares secrets through key pairs, a directory and inboxes, becomes a commercial service for moving secrets from A to B; shared keys are dropped because the easy two-word codes were found broken, recoverable offline from their public id; every person, browser and agent gets a key pair, the public key travels by link, QR code, email or WhatsApp, secrets come back encrypted as one-time drops, files or QR codes, and the private key lives in an identity vault unlocked by a passkey that a password manager keeps; most plumbing exists in SG/Send, append lanes and sgit pki, and the capabilities, not the transport, are what is charged for.

## [Handing secrets to agents and browsers: SG/Send's next focus, a key pair where the work runs, one-time drops, and a brief for a site that does only this](handing-secrets-to-agents.md)

2026-10-15 · Vaults & methodAgents & policy

Giving vault keys to browsers and scheduled agent sessions is the current pain, so SG/Send's technology should focus on one use case as a separate client-first site: the recipient makes its own key pair where it runs and shows the public half by QR code, link or text; the owner encrypts and signs; SG/Send holds the ciphertext for one download with deletion and expiry, which it already supports; the recipient verifies against a pinned owner key and pipes the secret into the tool, never into the model's context; it was run end to end locally; the first secret moves to the environment or a pairing step; and unlike API keys, which proxies keep out of agents, a vault key must reach the place that decrypts.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**12 nodes, 11 edges**

- **Secrets to sessions and browsers** (question) Vault keys by hand; passkeys that do not always reach.
- **Warned agents refuse** (example) The more the prompt insists, the more it refuses.
- **SG/Send already has it** (artefact) One download, deletion, expiry, client-side encryption; no location limit.
- **Short codes are broken** (claim) The public id is an unsalted hash of the code: recoverable offline.
- **The recipient makes the key** (method) Public half by QR code, link or text; owner encrypts and signs.
- **Into the tool, not the chat** (method) Decrypted into sgit clone; never in the prompt or transcript.
- **Tested end to end** (example) Decrypted once, 410 twice, signature verified, key unexportable.
- **The first secret** (question) From the environment, or a pairing step approved from a phone.
- **Against the trend** (claim) Proxies hide API keys; a vault key must reach the decrypter.
- **What exists** (concept) Send, share links, Yopass, PrivateBin, Wormhole, age.
- **SealDrop** (artefact) A working name; Handoff, KeyDrop, Courier, Baton are taken.
- **The brief** (artefact) One site, client first, pairing, no passphrase prompts.

> Anyone who uses the environment can read the values. Why the first secret is a choice about identity.

> The agent is never shown the secret, and never asked to be careful with it. The answer to the refusals.

2026-10-15 · Vaults & methodStartups & strategy

SG/Send began as file sharing where the server holds nothing, went live five days after its first commit, took payments within three weeks, and through folders, zips, a data room and the decision to copy Git became sgit and the vaults; the public record of 4,476 app commits, 1,620 command-line commits, 739 tags and 1,389 briefs corrects the founder's memory of the order, shows a fast February to May, a turn to focus in June, pauses and an October burst, shows the agents writing the code while the founder wrote briefs and merged, and records early that users bought credits and did not come back: the technology worked before the use case did.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**13 nodes, 11 edges**

- **The server holds nothing** (concept) Encrypted on the client; the key never sent.
- **Live in five days** (example) First commit 8 Feb; send.sgraph.ai live 13 Feb.
- **Ten paying customers** (example) Stripe on 1 Mar; £5 for 500 credits; 2 Mar.
- **Folders in 22 minutes** (example) Proposal 20:26, code 20:48, zip viewer 22:15.
- **The ideas came first** (claim) Vault and data room named in February, before the features.
- **Copy Git** (method) Commits, trees, refs, branches, encrypted; the client does the work.
- **Designing by simulation** (method) 6 revisions, 14 gaps found, 13 resolved, no code.
- **sgit** (artefact) The command on 16 Mar, the sgit-ai package on 20 Mar.
- **Vaults become apps** (artefact) Previews, HTML, sandboxed iframes, full screen by May.
- **The pace in the data** (claim) Commits on 246 of 249 days; bursts and pauses on the CLI.
- **Agents write, I merge** (claim) 1,298 of 1,671 commits under my name are merges.
- **Credits sit unused** (claim) Users bought, tested once and did not come back.
- **A real need now** (question) The same technology, with workflows that use it.

> stop inventing solutions to these problems. Git already solved all of them. Copy Git. The turning point, 4 March.

> Users buy credits, test once, and don't come back. Credits sit unused. What the market said, already on 5 March.

## [The tokens hook: a token behaviour policy that shows what every session reads, caches, writes and costs, why a prompt cannot do it, and a brief for tokens.hook.sgit.ai](the-tokens-hook.md)

2026-10-15 · Agents & policySite & engineering

Tokens deserve their own small agent behaviour policy, observe mode first: a Claude Code hook that reads only the new lines of the session transcript, counts each response once, prices it by model and shows the user a box of reads, cache share, writes, context and cost; asked through a prompt, the model correctly said it could not see its usage, while the hook gave exact figures one turn behind in about a millisecond; building it exposed double counting in our own session report and showed the transcript carries the system prompt and tool definitions; caching was 99% of this session's input, and the brief is a site, tokens.hook.sgit.ai, that treats one small hook as mission-critical code.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**12 nodes, 11 edges**

- **A token behaviour policy** (concept) Count, show, limit; observe first.
- **Caching is the bill** (claim) 99% of this session's input came from the cache.
- **Asking the model** (example) Twice it said it could not see the numbers.
- **The tokens hook** (artefact) 132 lines and a policy file; about 1 ms a call warm.
- **Exact, one turn behind** (claim) 37,087 tokens and $0.0484 against $0.0486 actual.
- **Usage repeats per block** (example) Counting lines gave 1.06B cache reads; responses gave 459M.
- **Our own report was wrong** (claim) The ABP block counted responses two or three times.
- **The transcript holds the request** (question) System prompt and 49 tool definitions, undocumented.
- **Who sees what** (method) systemMessage to the user, context to the model, block, log, lane.
- **Status line and OpenTelemetry** (method) Claude Code's own views, and a collector already built.
- **Other tools** (example) Hooks and usage commands in Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor; limits only in chat apps.
- **tokens.hook.sgit.ai** (artefact) Code, policy, graph, tests, numbers and releases for one hook.

> A prompt can ask for behaviour; only a hook can supply data The experiment in one line.

> A few percentage points of cache miss rate can dramatically affect cost and latency. Why tokens need a policy.

## [Cedar and the policy vault: a debrief on the policy language agents are adopting, where our behaviour policies and sgit vaults meet it, and a brief for the MVP](cedar-and-the-policy-vault.md)

2026-10-14 · Agents & policyVaults & method

Cedar, open-sourced by AWS in 2023, in the CNCF Sandbox since October 2025 and used by AgentCore Policy to check agent tool calls, already expresses most of an agent behaviour policy: permit for the grant, forbid for the barrier, entities for the footprint; it does not carry why a rule exists, which version was in force, or what it decided, and an sgit vault carries all three, as a local demo showed with a validation gate, signed tags, read-only enforcement clones and a sealed, hash-chained append lane of decisions; it also showed that Cedar skips a policy that errors, so an invalid forbid fails open, and the MVP must validate before release and deny on error.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**15 nodes, 15 edges**

- **Cedar** (concept) Open-source policy language and engine, formally modelled in Lean.
- **Mature and adopted** (claim) CNCF Sandbox since 8 October 2025; Verified Permissions, AgentCore Policy, Sondera.
- **AgentCore Policy** (example) Checks every agent tool call against Cedar before it runs.
- **Agent behaviour policy** (concept) Mandate, grant, barriers, layers.
- **Term by term** (artefact) Permit is the grant, forbid the barrier, entities the footprint.
- **Annotations as edges** (method) @abp_rule and @sbp_row join their graph to ours.
- **What Cedar does not carry** (claim) Why a rule exists, the version in force, the evidence.
- **Policy stores today** (example) Strict validation and IAM, but no history API and permanent deletion.
- **The policy vault** (artefact) Rules, schema, tests and decisions in one versioned, encrypted unit.
- **The gate** (method) Validate and test every version; v2 without its schema was refused.
- **An invalid forbid fails open** (claim) Cedar skips a policy that errors; deny on error.
- **Read-only enforcement** (method) Clone with the read key, load only a signed tag.
- **The evidence lane** (artefact) Sealed, hash-chained decisions, write-only for the decider.
- **Rules about history** (question) Session-aware policies need a history you can trust.
- **The MVP brief** (artefact) Eight steps, from the demo to a real hook and a report.

> No new Cedar version is released unless its model, proofs, and differential tests are current. Why Cedar is the mature place to connect to.

> A forbid that cannot be evaluated fails open. The sharp edge the demo found.
