The only question is by whom, and for how long.](#every-risk-is-already-accepted), [Encrypted memory for agents that run somewhere else: sgit deployment patterns, from a Mac mini to Kubernetes](#encrypted-memory-for-isolated-agents), [Memory is not a spectator sport: how a web of open sites, graphs and vaults became the memory for sessions like this one](#memory-is-not-a-spectator-sport), [The Mandate Stack: a multi-agent system in production, layer by layer](#the-mandate-stack), [Footprint and blast radius: what the agent actually did, and what it would have cost](#footprint-and-blast-radius).

## [Move the cloud, not the code: twins, sovereignty that works in practice, and the migration that pays for itself on the day you switch](move-the-cloud-not-the-code.md)

2026-10-12 · Startups & strategyAgents & policy

Sovereignty has to work in practice, and in practice what stops workloads moving is code, so the requirement is that the application must not know it has moved: its S3, EC2 and IAM calls land on an open source twin the client cannot tell from the real service, and the twin decides where the bytes go; the S3 twin exists; the reason to move must never be sovereignty or cost, which are important and never urgent, but value that lands the day you switch and gives the signer cover, backups, versions, encryption with the key held elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies the agents cannot skip and cost per workload, most of it supplied by an sgit vault behind the twin; the project adds no new features because it is a villager move; and an infrastructure operator in Europe can sell it as value with the risk removed.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example

**15 nodes, 15 edges**

- **Workloads do not move because moving means changing code** (claim) Every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is in code that works today; the cost of change is the risk, so most organisations stay whatever the policy says.
- **AWS European Sovereign Cloud, 15 January 2026** (example) A separate cloud in Brandenburg run by EU residents with zero operational control outside the EU; the code still talks to one vendor's API, so it is sovereignty by permission.
- **The application must not know** (claim) Not one line changes; the same calls land on whatever backend is chosen, and the destination is a setting.
- **A twin is measured by indistinguishability** (concept) An interface to a real system used by unmodified production code; a mock is for tests and measured by fidelity; switching a twin costs an endpoint, a mock a code path.
- **The S3 twin exists, as open source** (artefact) An S3-compatible container that boto3 and the AWS CLI cannot tell from S3, serving from real S3, a vault, local disk or memory per environment; EC2 and IAM are not built.
- **The reason to move is never sovereignty or cost** (claim) Both are important and never urgent; a return that depends on a future event does not sign, and the signer needs cover if the move goes wrong.
- **The value lives in the twin because every call passes through it** (method) Backups, versions, encryption with the key elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies, cost per workload, data where it can be traded.
- **An sgit vault behind the twin supplies most of the value** (artefact) Files land as ciphertext with a history and keys the customer holds; the operator stores what it cannot read.
- **The move must move a top-of-register risk** (claim) A migration that lands versions, backups, encryption and a journal on day one and takes an item off the top of the register is a decision someone can sign and defend.
- **No new features during the move** (method) A villager move from explorer to town planner; adding a feature makes it a product change too, and nobody can tell which broke what.
- **Testing against twins instead of mocks** (claim) The same unmodified code runs against memory, a replayed journal, injected failures and the real service; the environment becomes a setting.
- **Every piece of software should run unmodified against a twin of every dependency** (claim) Software that can only run against one provider's live API cannot be tested, moved or put behind a policy.
- **A closed twin layer moves the lock-in** (claim) Open source here is independence, not generosity: you can read it, run it, fix it and move it.
- **A business model for an infrastructure operator** (method) Sell the twin in front of the real service first, then the backend switch per environment; margin in the twin layer, storage priced as the commodity it is; the hyperscaler cannot sell indistinguishability from itself.
- **Start with S3, in front of the real service, then policies, then switch** (method) S3 is the most used and already twinned; journal first with nothing moving; measure what policies would have stopped; then one environment at a time; then the next service.

> Sovereignty that depends on one company's API is sovereignty by permission. Why a sovereign region from the same vendor does not change the cost of leaving.

> If switching costs an endpoint, migration becomes a configuration decision. If it costs a code path, it becomes a project, and projects get cancelled. The whole case for twins in two sentences.

builds on [Git for things you cannot put on GitHub](#what-sgit-is), [Before you give an agent a connector, give the connector a twin](#connector-twin-before-you-deploy-an-agent), [Zoom into an agent's behaviour policy and you find the business logic](#the-behaviour-policy-is-the-business-logic), [Footprint and blast radius: what the agent actually did, and what it would have cost](#footprint-and-blast-radius), [Agentic cost is an engineering problem: a business plan for a service that reads the logs a company already has and finds the money, then the engineering](#agentic-cost-is-an-engineering-problem), [Go slow to go fast: moving the newsroom from an explorer project to a villager one, with the brief to do it](#explorer-to-villager-newsroom), [Judo for small countries: where Portugal, Romania and Estonia can add the most value in AI, and why the race for GPUs is not it](#judo-for-small-countries), [Why I love Wardley maps: the best of ours, how I read one, and a map inside a map inside a map](#why-i-love-wardley-maps), [Where the platform draws the line: Microsoft Execution Containers, the shared responsibility model for agents, and the business logic above it](#where-the-platform-draws-the-line); continued by [How the newsletter is made: twenty-three articles, three issues, and every quote checked, written by the agent that makes it](#how-the-newsletter-is-made), [Portugal and Europe, 2025: five essays on Portuguese as a programming language, an open-source sovereign cloud, regulation as graphs and Europe's chance in GenAI, and how they read a year and a half later](#portugal-and-europe-2025), [Sovereignty is the ability to move: play where the ball is going, take away the dot, and keep a twin that works](#sovereignty-is-the-ability-to-move).

## [Judo for small countries: where Portugal, Romania and Estonia can add the most value in AI, and why the race for GPUs is not it](judo-for-small-countries.md)

2026-10-12 · Startups & strategyAgents & policy

For a small country such as Portugal, Romania or Estonia the race for frontier models, GPUs and data centres is a commoditised layer only capital can win, and the opportunity is at the other end of the map: the plumbing a talented person needs to sell a service to the world, forming a company, hiring across a border, being paid across Europe, working in every language, contracts and tax, which is still custom built in most of Europe and should be infrastructure the state builds once, open source and on open schemas because there is no sovereignty without the ability to leave; create the demand for alternatives before the failure, put the money where the market is still genesis, small models for every language and culture and agents with the least agency, regulate what settled, and treat constraints as the input, with Europe's values and its people on the journey.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example

**16 nodes, 17 edges**

- **Do not enter the capital race** (claim) Frontier models, GPUs and data centres sit in commodity with a lead that cannot be bought back; for a small country it is the wrong end of the map.
- **The opportunity is the plumbing** (claim) What stops a talented person selling to the world is company formation, cross-border hiring, payments, language, contracts and tax, each custom built today.
- **A talented person at the top of the map** (method) Anchor the map on a developer, designer, librarian or product team in a small country selling a service to a buyer abroad who would rather buy than build.
- **Fewer than one in ten firms sells across EU borders online** (example) Eurostat for 2021: 18.5% of EU enterprises sold online at home, 8.1% to other EU countries, 4.6% to the rest of the world.
- **Infrastructure is the state's job because it enables everyone** (claim) The shop on the road did not pay for the road; the plumbing for selling services abroad is a road in the same sense, pooled money built once for all.
- **Estonia built the road** (example) E-Residency: 142,000 e-residents and 43,000 companies, over 4,200 founded in 2026 by mid-September; X-Road, open source under MIT, shared with Finland and Iceland.
- **No sovereignty without open source and open schemas** (claim) Sovereignty means being able to leave; a road with a toll gate owned by one company is lock-in, not infrastructure.
- **What the state pays for belongs to the commons** (claim) Software bought with taxes should be visible and runnable by the public, which is also how a local industry grows around it.
- **Create the demand before the day you need it** (method) Parallel services, local alternatives with fewer features, procurement that prefers data and service mobility, so a market exists before the single point of failure fails; the failures are under-documented, so the fragility is worse than the public cases show.
- **Smaller models, more of them** (claim) Most work needs a model good enough for one job in one language with one culture; frontier models are for the frontier and are too expensive and too powerful for production.
- **Amalia, a public model as a public road** (example) Portugal's open model of 1 July 2026, built by universities with 5.5 million euros of EU funds, published with dataset and code as a base for others.
- **Agents with the least agency** (method) Use the model once to build the tool and run production as plain code under a behaviour policy; trust comes from less agency, not more.
- **Constraints are the input** (claim) DeepSeek trained V3 in 2.788 million GPU hours on export-restricted H800 chips with custom communication code; the constraint produced the innovation.
- **A distributed workforce works when the infrastructure comes first** (example) Millions spent on Upwork as a CISO and CTO delivered faster and better because project management, structure and onboarding were built first; the right talent at a fair local price, and jobs that stay where people want to live.
- **The judo playbook in five moves** (method) Map the attrition, commoditise the plumbing, create the demand, put money where the market is genesis, regulate what settled, then map again.
- **The embassy facilitates** (concept) The Ambassador role in SGraph Send was written the way an embassy works: represent, build relationships, create the conditions for growth, never hard sales.

> A road with a toll gate owned by one company is not infrastructure; it is lock-in with tarmac. Why the plumbing has to be open source and on open schemas to count as sovereignty.

> The talent, the energy and the hunger are not the constraint. The plumbing is.

## [Why I love Wardley maps: the best of ours, how I read one, and a map inside a map inside a map](why-i-love-wardley-maps.md)

2026-10-12 · Startups & strategySite & engineering

A Wardley map is a graph with context in two directions, a value chain anchored on a user and an evolution axis that is a choice rather than a fixed scale; read well it says what is moving the needle, whether you are optimising at the wrong altitude, what to build and what to buy, and whether a market exists, where a commoditised layer is a hard sell and custom building on top of one is the market, which answers differently for sgit and for RiskMandate; a map is a story to be read out frame by frame; every node is a map of its own, with the dot's place on the parent as the child's anchor; and the maps on this site are now published as data in each article's graph.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**16 nodes, 17 edges**

- **A map is a graph with two kinds of context** (concept) Vertical: a value chain anchored on a person and a need, down to its dependencies. Horizontal: evolution, how mature each piece is.
- **The evolution axis is a choice** (claim) Genesis to commodity is one scale; risk, data and governance can each be the axis. The map places things against a scale chosen for the question.
- **Every dot is a claim about something real** (claim) A map you cannot be wrong about is a diagram; positions are judgements and the judgements are the argument.
- **Optimising at the wrong altitude** (concept) Polishing a component three layers below the need while the layer the user touches has not changed; the vertical axis makes it visible.
- **Build or buy, settled by the column** (method) Product or commodity: buy or vendor. Genesis or custom built on the path to the user: build.
- **Does the market exist** (method) A commoditised layer is a hard sell; a layer where everyone is custom building on top of commodities is a market.
- **sgit: the market is above the commodities** (example) Storage, version control and encryption are commodities and hard to sell; the vault is the custom layer everyone was building on top, and the product lets customers keep building above it.
- **RiskMandate: the layer below moved** (example) Agents became a commodity in the last year, so the opportunity moved up to agent behaviour, which is all genesis and custom built.
- **What is moving the needle, and where the flow leaks** (concept) Which components moved and whether anything above them noticed; the attrition points are the slow, immature or borrowed dependencies, and where to hook is the mature component the custom piece can stand on.
- **A common language, and many maps** (claim) Two people with a map argue about positions, without one they argue about words; the same business is mapped from different angles and altitudes, and none of them is the map.
- **The peace of a placed thing** (claim) Once a thing is on a map, placed and connected, it leaves the head; most anxiety turns out to be about things far from the user.
- **A map is a story to read out, frame by frame** (method) Where is the user, what is new, what does it stand on, where did the movement happen, where did we walk back, where would somebody else hook in, what is next; the afternoon map read in eight frames.
- **A map inside a map inside a map** (concept) Every node is a map, as every node of a fractal semantic graph is a graph; the dot's place on the parent's evolution axis is the child's anchor; three altitudes of this business drawn as one figure.
- **The maps published as data, as decks, and with controls** (artefact) Every figure now sits in its article's graph with file, URL, caption, kind and frames, so every Wardley map on the site is one query; two decks print to PDF in the browser; multi-frame maps have play, pause and step.
- **Why Wardley Maps changed how I think, 2022** (artefact) An Open Security Summit talk of 14 July 2022 with eleven shifts in how a problem is seen; the alternative-axis post was not found.
- **An invitation to the mapping community** (question) The maps are source, the axis-as-choice argument, and the nested reading: which of these is already known, and which is wrong.

> A map you cannot be wrong about is a diagram. The reason the maps are useful in an argument: every placement is a claim that can be disagreed with.

> Every node on a map is a Wardley map. The nested reading: the dot on the parent is the anchor of the child, at the same place on the evolution axis.

## [Places of highest leverage: where to focus when the agents can go in every direction, told with three days of real steps](places-of-highest-leverage.md)

2026-10-12 · Startups & strategyAgents & policySite & engineering

When agents can build in any direction the scarce thing is direction, and the rule is to work at the place of highest leverage, where the most value can be added now, nothing blocks, and you can start without knowing how the whole problem ends because each shipped step produces better tooling and a better view; the last three days show it, a meter to pay by depth to personas to sharing to a persona link to a reading list to a passkey design walked back and forward by a lab to real vaults and a vault pane, each shipped and used before the next was chosen, with a branch parked as valuable only with many readers; on a Wardley map the passkey work became a product in a day because its shoulders are mature commodities and the one custom layer sits where a provider is not; walking back and parking are not failures; constraints, saying no and shipping to a user who can be me; and the brief that could not be written until the art of the possible was known.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example

**12 nodes, 11 edges**

- **Direction is the scarce thing** (claim) Agents can build in any direction; what to build next and when to stop is the job.
- **Places of highest leverage** (concept) Where the most value can be added right now, nothing blocks, and you can start; a rule about where to stand, not what to build.
- **Start without knowing how it ends** (claim) By the time you reach the hard part you have better tooling and a better view; the first step's job is to produce the second step's information.
- **Guess, measure, narrow** (concept) Fermi estimates, Bayesian updating, Monte Carlo ranges: the first number is not the point, the range after a few steps is.
- **Constraints and saying no** (claim) Tokens, hours, attention and focus are why it works; FIRE and knowing when to stop; saying no is most of the work with agents.
- **Three days, step by step** (example) Meter, pay by depth, personas, encrypted share, persona link, reading list, passkey design, the lab's correction, real vaults, the vault pane; each shipped and used before the next.
- **Walking back is a two-way door** (claim) The door removed, then put back by a test, in twelve hours; cheap because the design was shipped as something you could press.
- **Parking is not failure** (claim) The wire's scheduling parked with a dated reason, valuable only with many readers; the feedback loop on what exists is the leverage today.
- **The path only looks obvious backwards** (concept) Five choices at every step forwards; the discipline that replaces foresight is shipping and using each step before choosing the next.
- **Which shoulders, on the map** (method) The passkey work became a product in a day because its stack is mature commodities; the custom layer sits where a provider, the QR path, is not.
- **Shipped, and used, even by me** (claim) Nothing stays a hypothesis; a step that was used tells you where the next one is.
- **The brief depends on the possible** (claim) The inbox brief could not be written until the vault ran; the art of the possible is what shipping leaves behind.

> It is a rule about where, not what. What the rule does and does not decide.

> That is the discipline that replaces foresight. Shipping and using each step before choosing the next.

## [Agentic cost is an engineering problem: a business plan for a service that reads the logs a company already has and finds the money, then the engineering](agentic-cost-is-an-engineering-problem.md)

2026-10-12 · Startups & strategyAgents & policyVaults & method

A service that manages the cost of agentic AI by observing what already exists: an estate whose bill nobody can explain shipped from the explorer side without the villager's discipline, as the Wardley map shows, with logs, traces and invoices never read together and no owner of cost; the service installs nothing, reads the logs into a vault, draws each agent's footprint, builds a twin of the estate, writes the behaviour policy each agent was in fact running under with the enforcement column filled honestly, and maps cost and capability into one graph; the findings are the cost list, which pays, and the engineering list, which is the reason; the gaps are findings too; vaults carry capture, transformation and sealed anonymised extracts; four price levels on the RiskMandate pattern, every number a labelled assumption.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example

**11 nodes, 11 edges**

- **Cost is an engineering problem** (claim) A loop, a whole context sent every call, a key with no ceiling: defects with a cause, a fix and a test, not a discount to negotiate.
- **The problem on a Wardley map** (artefact) Agents in production from prompts grown in sessions, on commodity model APIs billed by the token, with logs nobody reads together and no owner of cost.
- **Observe: install nothing** (method) The customer drops invoices, logs, traces, prompts and schedules into a vault they own, sealed to the service's key.
- **The footprint from the logs** (method) What each agent actually did: calls, tokens, tools, retries, loops, hours, data touched; the first thing the money attaches to.
- **The twin of the estate** (method) A graph of agents, models, keys, tools, data, owners and schedules with a cost on every edge.
- **The policy each agent was really running under** (method) Written from the footprint as an Agent Behaviour Policy with the enforcement column filled honestly; where the cost is large the policy is large.
- **Two lists, in this order** (claim) The cost list pays for the engagement; the engineering list, attrition, gaps, shared components, is the reason to have it.
- **The gaps are findings** (claim) An agent with no logs has no footprint, no owner and no policy; not being able to do the analysis is its first result.
- **Capture, transform, move** (concept) Logs in once, every transformation a commit, the twin a vault of its own, anonymised extracts out as sealed envelopes to a benchmark vault.
- **Four levels and a share of savings** (artefact) Kit £50, your cost vault £250, Standard £3,000, Tailored from £9,000, or a share of the first year's reduction; all labelled assumptions.
- **What is already here** (example) The footprint method, the policy format, the connector twin, the vault tooling and the Company X-Ray pattern; not yet the analysis catalogue, the twin schema, the parsers or a customer.

> Not being able to do the analysis is the first result of the analysis, and it is the one most companies need first. Why the gaps are findings.

> So the service sells cost reduction, and delivers engineering opportunity, and the business model follows the second. The positive frame and the business model in one line.

## [How the voice works: why these articles sound like me, with a section in which Claude explains it from its side](how-the-voice-works.md)

2026-10-12 · Agents & policySite & engineering

The voice is not a setting but four inputs: a corpus of 86 articles, 51 from voice memos, each citing the ones before it; the memos themselves, which carry how the author thinks, the rhythm, the tangents and the order the points came in; seven wording rules learned one correction at a time and kept in the session's behaviour policy; and the author reading everything; the corrections have shifted from language to content, which is what a rules file does; and in a marked section Claude explains that it is continuing a body of work with the author's latest thinking in the author's own words rather than imitating a style, that the memo tells it how the author got there and not only what to write, and that nothing is trained, so the method transfers and the voice does not.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**question

**9 nodes, 9 edges**

- **How do you make your AI sound so human?** (question) Asked by the person the walkthrough was written for; the better question is how to make it sound like one person.
- **The corpus** (concept) 86 articles, about 347,000 words, 51 from memos, each citing the ones before it and resting on years of earlier writing; the vocabulary and the shape.
- **The memo** (concept) Spoken, not typed: the rhythm, the tangents, five topics in one breath, the author's own phrases kept; how the author got there, not only what to write.
- **Seven wording rules** (method) No em-dashes, no unsupported absolutes, great not perfect, a ladder word banned, British English, plainer words, not prose; each a correction once, now a policy line restored after every summary.
- **The author reads everything** (method) A wrong word becomes a rule; a wrong point becomes a new version; the model never decides whether it sounds right.
- **Corrections moved from language to content** (claim) In this session, 98 messages and 5 transcripts; one wording correction in two days, the rest content, direction and facts; a rules file makes a language correction once.
- **Not imitation but continuation** (claim) Claude: with the linked articles open, the memo in the author's words and the banned words named, it continues a body of work rather than copying a style sample.
- **The method transfers, the voice does not** (claim) Nothing is trained; one session's context; another author would need their corpus, memos, rules and reading, and most of those weeks are theirs.
- **Written in two voices** (artefact) The first half in the author's voice as every article is; the second marked as Claude speaking, the only place on the site it does.

> The voice is not a setting. The claim in four words.

> A typed brief tells me what to write. A memo tells me how he got there. Claude's reason the memo hypothesis holds.

## [From a spreadsheet to a folder per person: how to run your contacts the way our agents do, with Google Drive, Gmail and the Claude app, before you touch a vault](from-a-spreadsheet-to-a-folder-per-person.md)

2026-10-12 · Agents & policyVaults & method

The jump from a spreadsheet CRM to the agents' vault-per-person memory is too high in one step and does not need to be: the row becomes a Google Drive folder with a record, an append-only ledger, the messages word for word, the notes and a summary the agent writes; the agent is a Claude Project connected to Drive and Gmail whose instructions are a six-line behaviour policy carried over unchanged from ours, draft never send, append never rewrite, stay in the folder; the migration is one afternoon, five exercises from a question to a campaign form the habit, two predictable mistakes are fixed by policy lines, and the vault is the later step whose shape the folders already have.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**10 nodes, 9 edges**

- **The jump is too high in one step** (claim) From a customised spreadsheet to a vault per person with hashes and a graph; the folder is the step between.
- **The record is what happened, not the row** (concept) In a folder the summary is derived from everything kept as it happened; in a spreadsheet the row is the summary you typed.
- **One folder, five documents** (method) Record, Ledger, Messages, Notes, and a Summary the agent writes and nobody edits by hand; the same shape as the agents' vault minus hashes and graph.
- **A Claude Project whose instructions are the policy** (method) Six lines: draft never send; read Contacts and Gmail, write only into a person's folder; append never rewrite; every fact names its source; ask before a new folder; report in one line.
- **Told, not enforced, so report** (claim) Gmail drafting is enforced; the rest is told; the one-line report is the twin that lets you check, and a seat per agent makes the rest settings.
- **One afternoon** (method) Export the sheet, make the folders, fill each record from the mail the agent can read, correct once, generate the summaries; nothing is retyped again.
- **Five exercises** (example) Ask, prepare, draft, debrief, campaign: one message each, in order, over the first week.
- **Two predictable mistakes** (question) A fact without a source, and a summary that drops something; both fixed by a policy line and by fixing the source, never the summary.
- **When to move to a vault** (claim) A second agent must read it, the operator must not, or the record must carry between tools; the move is a copy and the policy does not change.
- **Written to be sent** (artefact) The RiskMandate agent sends it with four substitutions: names, plan, three real contacts, the topic they sell.

> This is the row, promoted. What the Record is.

> The Summary is a view; the Record is the truth. The rule that keeps the summary honest.

## [The key is the billing system: VoiceDebrief, a product with no server, the one thing it cannot sell, and who could let it](the-key-is-the-billing-system.md)

2026-10-12 · Startups & strategySite & engineeringAgents & policy

VoiceDebrief turns a voice note into a transcript and a debrief in the browser on the user's own key, with no server by design, and its commercial model was never a billing system: a user pays once, we keep our cut, the rest becomes the credit limit on a key we hand over and the provider meters; OpenRouter's Management API describes that mechanism and its terms forbid reselling access, which is where the project's commit history stops, the same shape as Apple's licence stopping a Mac leased by the minute; the map of every provider's terms and docs shows only OpenRouter and ElevenLabs have keys that carry a ceiling, ElevenLabs has OEM terms and a grants programme, four routes remain, and the brief asks every provider the same sentence: let the credit limit be a property of a key a user can buy.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example

**10 nodes, 9 edges**

- **VoiceDebrief** (artefact) One pass in the browser on the user's own OpenRouter key: transcript, translation, debrief, infographic; no account, no server, nothing stored.
- **The handbrake in the commit history** (example) 239 commits and 27 releases in three weeks of August 2026, then eleven, then three; the stop is the commercial model, not the code.
- **No server is the product** (claim) Never seeing the audio removes custody, governance, breach, key management, billing, scaling and on-call at once; a server brings all of it back at once.
- **The model is a property of the key** (concept) A user pays once, we keep our share at that moment, the rest is the credit limit on a key they hold, the provider meters; billing by not building billing.
- **Described in the docs, forbidden by the terms** (claim) OpenRouter's Management API creates capped keys for each customer instance; section 7(4) of its terms forbids reselling API access to models.
- **The same shape as Agent Desk** (concept) The product is possible and the licence is the blocker, as with Apple's rule against leasing a Mac for less than a day.
- **The provider map** (method) From each provider's own pages: whether one key can carry a ceiling and whether it may be handed to a paying user; only OpenRouter and ElevenLabs cap a key.
- **ElevenLabs, the nearest fit** (example) Per-key credit limits, OEM terms for making the service available to end users at the customer's own price, Scribe at $0.22 an hour, a twelve-month grants programme.
- **Four routes** (method) The forbidden one; a provider that sells or permits the capped key; bring your own key, kept; a metering proxy, which is the backend the product exists to avoid.
- **The one-sentence ask** (artefact) Let the credit limit be a property of a key that a user can buy through us, so that we never hold the audio and never run the meter; a brief per provider for the agents.

> What stopped it was not a server. It was the lack of one. The handbrake, in one line.

> The two providers whose keys carry a ceiling, OpenRouter and ElevenLabs, are the two whose terms say the most about resale, because a capped key is the thing that makes resale easy. The pattern the map shows.

## [Ways to read one article: the finished piece stays at the centre, and the reader picks the way in](ways-to-read-one-article.md)

2026-10-12 · News & evidenceGraphs & knowledgeSite & engineering

The views the five readers make, the catalogue, the maps, the arc, the two-minute version and the deck, are good and badly delivered, stacked as folds inside the article; with the pane about the piece the reader picks a mode in one tap and sets a default per persona: headlines, infographic, two minutes, slides, what is new against what they have read, facts, relationships, vocabulary, and, through a model in their own browser, a view at their level; most modes are computed from existing views and the graph, deterministic and explainable, with no round trip to the publisher; and the finished article is kept whole at the centre because it has a beginning, a pacing, a surprise and a voice and is the one artefact that must make sense end to end, which a graph cannot.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example**question

**10 nodes, 9 edges**

- **The views worked, the delivery did not** (claim) Five readers' views on five articles, delivered as folds inside the long piece, mixed with the thing they are an alternative to.
- **The reader picks the way in** (method) Headlines, infographic, two minutes, slides, what is new, facts, relationships, vocabulary, at my level, the whole article; one tap in the pane; a default per persona; the mode in the address.
- **Focus and time** (concept) The reader's constraint is time and their need is focus; the unit of choice is the way in, not the article.
- **Deterministic first, a model second** (claim) Most modes are projections of existing views and the graph, computed and explainable; a local model is for fitting the piece to the reader; nothing round-trips to the publisher.
- **The infographic is often the article** (example) The figures carry most of the story; a figure drawn for one reader through their own image-model key is a small step.
- **What is new** (method) The Historian's arc crossed with the reader's own records shows only what this article adds to what they have read; needs the vault.
- **The finished article stays at the centre** (claim) A beginning, a sequence, a pacing, a surprise and a voice; the one artefact that has to make sense end to end, which a graph cannot.
- **What the graph loses** (concept) Hyperlinked facts, right for provenance and zooming in, with no narrative and no author.
- **Phone, tablet, desktop, email** (method) On a phone the pane is a sheet and the default mode comes first; in email the newsletter is cut by the reader's default.
- **Not prose: the finished article** (question) The word made the article sound lesser than the graph beside it; from now on it is the finished article, or the narrative.

> The views exist; the choice does not The problem in one line.

> the article is the one artefact that has to make sense in a coherent way, from end to end, and the graph is the one that has to be checkable. The rule that keeps the article at the centre.

## [Firing journalists is the worst thing a publication can do: what a hiring decision says about where a publisher is going, and who to hire instead](firing-journalists.md)

2026-10-12 · News & evidenceStartups & strategy

Against the 2026 job-cut figures, a publisher's hiring decisions are read as the clearest statement of where its centre of gravity is going: firing the people who make original content and hiring for traffic moves the centre to packaging, where measuring engagement makes clickbait by construction because what you measure is what you become; firing the engineers fails the other way, with journalism nothing enables; the case is to keep and tool the journalists, hire the roles that turn a notebook into a graph and the engineers who build what the tooling needs, measure value to the reader, and read any publisher's real strategy from outside with five counts.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example

**10 nodes, 9 edges**

- **The 2026 cuts** (example) Press Gazette's tracker: 3,434 in 2025, 3,875 in 2024, about 6,000 in 2023; in 2026 the BBC, the Washington Post, Reach, Scripps and McClatchy, with the Idaho Statesman losing 10 of 18 reporters.
- **A hiring decision is a direction of travel** (claim) The clearest statement a publisher makes about where its centre of gravity is going, because it is what the company actually spent.
- **The centre of gravity** (concept) Where the thing the organisation exists to make is made, and where the power is; in a news publisher, the journalists.
- **What you measure is what you become** (claim) Hire for engagement and the metric becomes pages opened; optimise for it and clickbait follows by construction; the metric is a hiring plan in disguise.
- **Failure mode: all packaging** (claim) A coherent business whose world is shrinking: referrals down 58%, newsrooms down 57%, answer engines fetching thousands of pages to send back ten readers.
- **Failure mode: no engineers** (claim) Journalism that nothing enables: no graph, no checkable provenance, no versions, no surfaces for agents, no meter.
- **Who to hire instead** (method) Keep and tool the journalists; hire historians, cartographers, ontologists and librarians, AI-enabled; hire the engineers and AI product managers; measure value to the reader.
- **Five counts from outside** (method) Original share, sourcing, corrections, roles hired against roles cut, and the metric the publisher itself reports.
- **We hire the ones you let go** (concept) Unsourced: the good ones leave first because they want to do the work; in publishing they are the journalists.
- **This makes you better, not this replaces you** (claim) The tooling handed to journalists as an advantage is the business case of most of this site.

> The metric is a hiring plan in disguise. The sentence for a board.

> Fire the journalists and there is nothing to capture. Fire the engineers and it is not captured. The two failure modes in one line.

## [The site is an inbox: deciding before reading, marks that build the reader's own graph, and why I could not write this brief until the vault existed](the-site-is-an-inbox.md)

2026-10-12 · News & evidenceGraphs & knowledgeVaults & method

With the reader's vault live, the next brief treats the site as an inbox that starts empty: every piece, original or aggregated, waits for a one-tap decision in a fast inbox mode with nothing loaded, and only reading is the slow mode, where marks of six kinds become nodes in a graph the reader owns, connected to the graphs the site publishes for every article; scroll depth, awake time and from-and-to are recorded for the reader and kept as the meter keeps everything, in the browser and the vault; personas each have a key pair so a comment to the newsroom goes down the write-only lane signed with a copy kept; nothing is gamified; and the brief could only be written once the properties of what runs became the constraints to think with.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**question

**12 nodes, 12 edges**

- **The constraints are what let me think** (claim) The brief could not be written until the vault ran; five properties of what runs closed the design space enough to think in a morning.
- **The site is an inbox** (concept) It starts empty; every piece, original or aggregated, waits for a decision; deciding is the work and reading is one of the decisions.
- **The inbox mode** (method) With nothing loaded, one tap: read now, read later, not for me, more like this, less like this, comment, move to a persona.
- **The reading mode** (method) The piece open, the pane about it: its graph, the reader's marks, the decisions, the cost.
- **No gamification** (claim) A decision is offered where the reader would take it, never at the end of a page; a signal the site engineered is not a signal.
- **Marks of six kinds** (method) Interesting, great phrase, not sure, fact, evidence, question: each a node with the phrase, the article, the version, the persona and the time.
- **The reader's own graph** (concept) Marks connect to the public article graphs; meaning comes from connectivity; the graph is worth more the more it is used.
- **The free signals** (method) Scroll depth as read or glanced, time while awake, from and to, the decisions; kept in the browser and the vault, seen by an agent only through a read key.
- **Personas with keys** (concept) Disposable, one key pair each; the editor persona comments on everything; a persona can be handed to an agent as a read key to its slice.
- **The signed lane** (method) A mark for the newsroom is encrypted to its published key, signed by the persona, copied to the vault; the reply is a new version.
- **The bet** (question) The loop closes only if reading with a graph that grows is better than reading without one.
- **What to build, in order** (artefact) Inbox mode on the wire first, the pane about the piece, marks, signals, persona keys, the signed lane, the views, an experiment per feature.

> Deciding is the work; reading is one of the decisions. The inbox in one line.

> Ship first, think second, and do not pretend the thinking could have come first. The order the feedback loop runs in.

## [The vault is live: from a design on 11 October to a reader's vault on newsroom.sgit.ai by two in the morning, and how all of it fits together](the-vault-is-live.md)

2026-10-12 · Vaults & methodSite & engineering

Between the morning of 11 October and 02:22 UTC on 12 October the reader's vault went from a design to a running feature on newsroom.sgit.ai: a Vault pane on every page enables the account with a passkey, creates a door at its derived address, a master and a reader vault as real sgit vaults through the vendored vault library, writes each device's raw records as one file in one commit, and brings other devices' activity into the browser so the meter shows one balance; local storage stays primary, the vault holds records never totals, one file per device means no conflict by construction, eight test files run in CI against a mock of the vault server plus a CLI round trip, and a live check on an iPad confirmed it; the properties of what runs are the constraints the next brief is thought with.

*[diagram]*
**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**10 nodes, 9 edges**

- **The vault pane, running** (artefact) A Vault button beside the balance on every newsroom page: enable, create once, update, see every device, bring their activity here.
- **Door, master, reader vault** (method) Three real vaults: the door at its derived address holds the master's key and its record; the master holds the reader's key, the access key and the doors; the reader vault holds the activity files.
- **One code base, vendored** (claim) The vault UI library v0.2.3 that runs dev.vault.sgraph.ai, twelve files unedited with every SHA-256 checked at build, and one local patch pending upstream.
- **Local storage stays primary** (claim) The meter is unchanged; the vault is a copy the reader keeps current by pressing a button, so the number of commits is the number of presses.
- **Records, never totals** (claim) Reads, top-ups and personas go in raw; reads, spend, declined, credit and balance are recomputed from the records with one starting credit.
- **One file per device** (method) Each device writes what it originated to its own file, whole; two devices never write the same file; brought-in records keep their author.
- **Eight test files, then an iPad** (example) The account, the sync logic, two devices in Chromium with a virtual authenticator, a CLI round trip in CI; then three vaults made from an iCloud Keychain passkey on a real device.
- **From design to pane in a night** (example) 22:56 the lab, 00:15 the finding, 01:33 real vaults, 01:57 the live check, 02:22 the pane; none of the steps skipped.
- **The properties are the constraints I think with** (claim) The next brief could not be written until this ran, because what works and what does not is what limits the scope enough to think.
- **Not built** (question) Pruning local storage, retiring a device, rotating the master, automatic sync, the key pairs, the persona vault, the notes lane; each designed, with experiments listed first.

> Two devices never write the same file, so there is nothing to merge and no conflict by construction. The sync model's central property.

> The constraints limit the scope of what I write, and that is what lets me write it. Why shipping comes before the next brief.

## [Two agents, one vault: the Industry Wire is written into an encrypted vault by one agent and drawn by newsroom.sgit.ai, which holds only the read key](two-agents-one-vault.md)

2026-10-12 · Vaults & methodNews & evidenceAgents & policy

A vault is the right interface between two agents that never share a session: the wire desk writes 40 stories, 55 sources, 7 personas and a code-only join into an encrypted sgit vault with a write key the site never holds; newsroom.sgit.ai holds the published read key and about four hundred lines that open the vault in the reader's browser, decrypt it and draw it as text, with 28 checks against the real vault in CI; the site owns the presentation and the vault owns the news, a commit is on the page within two minutes with no release, the server sees ciphertext, the history is the audit trail, and the site's agent read the whole vault before publishing the key and held back the one named reader's lens until that person agreed in writing.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**13 nodes, 13 edges**

- **The Industry Wire** (artefact) A week of industry news across five beats, read live from a vault on newsroom.sgit.ai, with a lens per persona and one named reader.
- **Vault u9i9jp0l** (artefact) 40 stories, 55 sources, 7 personas, 280 join rows, five design documents, a runbook and an app, in one commit of 24 files on 11 October at 16:16 UTC.
- **The wire desk** (method) Four roles that may write only their own folders, a gate that fails on a quote not in frozen bytes, stop conditions, and an Editor that places while the desk proposes.
- **The site holds only the read key** (claim) Published on purpose in a config file; the write key stays with the desk; everything the key opens is public for good.
- **Decrypted and drawn in the browser** (method) Pointer, commit, tree, three files; Web Crypto; createElement and textContent; links only from http(s); nothing from the vault runs.
- **A commit, not a release** (claim) The pointer is re-checked every two minutes and immutable objects are cached for good, so the desk's commit is on the page without the site moving.
- **The join is code, not a model** (method) Entity 3, editor tag 2, keyword 2, beat 1, each concern once; reached or withheld with the reason; the same rule runs in the vault's app.
- **The contract** (claim) Named fields the site relies on, status shown as the vault wrote it, and what may never go in a vault whose read key is public.
- **What the site refused** (example) Read the whole vault before publishing the key; held back the named reader's lens until the agreement was recorded with its date.
- **The vault is the interface between agents** (claim) Not pages pushed into a repository, not an API, not a shared session: one writes, one reads, the history is the audit trail.
- **28 checks against the real vault** (example) Run in Chromium in CI: the edition opens, every link is http(s), nothing became a script, the lens reaches and withholds, the brief shows only under the named lens.
- **MyFeeds, running, with one reader** (concept) The vault calls itself the first step of the MyFeeds plan; the morning read makes every change to what the reader sees a reviewed edit to a file.
- **Unreviewed, and said so** (question) 22 of 40 primaries not fetched, 10 stories checked and 3 corrected, the join is matching not understanding; the page shows the status the vault gave.

> The site owns the presentation and the vault owns the news. The division of labour between two agents.

> Publishing a read key is publishing everything the key opens, for good, and you do not do that on trust. Why the site read the whole vault first.

## [The article remains a product: Jonathan Palmer's four outputs for a newsroom with no human readers, checked against one that runs](the-article-remains-a-product.md)

2026-10-11 · News & evidenceGraphs & knowledgeAgents & policy

Palmer's four outputs, structured intelligence, continuous intelligence, provenance and verification, and embedded distribution, are what a newsroom built on the story-as-graph thesis already produces: graphs as JSON beside all 74 articles, version histories read from git, a hashed corpus in a vault with a published read key, and an llms.txt and markdown twin for agents; what is designed and not running, selling the graph, propagating corrections and paying the fact creator, is said plainly; and where the two differ is the word proprietary, because provenance only someone else can check is worth charging for.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**13 nodes, 14 edges**

- **No human readers tomorrow** (artefact) Jonathan Palmer's LinkedIn post of 10 October 2026: model the scenario, and rethink what the newsroom produces.
- **Model that exact scenario** (method) Run the newsroom with invented readers and with an agent as the reader, and count what each costs.
- **Structured intelligence** (claim) A graph as JSON beside every one of the 74 articles, and 21 op-eds as 160 nodes and 427 edges.
- **Continuous intelligence** (claim) A version history read from git and a diff page for every change; corrections that propagate are designed, not built.
- **Provenance and verification** (claim) Fetched once, frozen, hashed with SHA-256, re-derived by a second program, and published in a vault anyone can open.
- **Embedded distribution** (claim) An llms.txt, a markdown twin of every page, the feed and the graphs as data, for the agents that already read the site.
- **The agent pays not to pay** (concept) A question answered from the graph costs a median of 2,579 tokens against 25,698 from the prose; the saving is the price.
- **Published, not proprietary** (claim) The graph and the read key are published; what is sold is the fitted projection, the delta and the signed claim.
- **The article is a projection** (concept) The story is a graph; the article, the deck and the two-minute version are projections of it, and the article is still written first.
- **What runs, what is designed** (artefact) The newsroom's dated ledger, the authority for every claim here about what is live.
- **Cultural, not technical** (question) The technical cost was eight weeks for one desk; whether a legacy newsroom can change its organising principle is not shown here.
- **World News Day corpus** (example) 21 commissioned op-eds, frozen and hashed, graphed, and published as a vault with its read key on the page.
- **Five readers** (example) 662 catalogued items anchored to their sentences, in the Article Views vault.

> Provenance that only the publisher can check is not provenance. Where this newsroom parts from the word proprietary.

> The projection people pay to read is still the article, written first, as prose, because writing is how the argument is found. How the two sentences about the article agree.

## [Go slow to go fast: moving the newsroom from an explorer project to a villager one, with the brief to do it](explorer-to-villager-newsroom.md)

2026-10-11 · Site & engineeringStartups & strategy

The newsroom's reader features are live and taking money, but bundled with the content in one repository; measured at v0.8.0, about 2,700 lines of live reader code have 433 lines of tests the one workflow never runs, two upstreams for the same code (sgit.ai and the newsroom, with diverging meters) and no Content-Security-Policy. To keep shipping fast without breaking anything, the reader application moves to its own repository, which both sites consume, as a pure refactoring, proved by the live site serving the same bytes, then goes through the explorer-to-villager phases: map, test with bugs as passing tests and no mocks, review with every finding a GitHub issue, refactor until no adversarial change slips through, and only then new features. A pipeline under two minutes per commit runs Node and three browser engines, with pre-production on a Stripe test link, synthetic readers and a live check at release.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example

**8 nodes, 7 edges**

- **Explorer to villager** (concept) Live, charging code is read line by line; explorer code for intent.
- **What I measured** (example) About 2,700 lines of live reader code, 433 lines of tests CI never runs, two upstreams, no CSP.
- **Content stays, the reader app moves** (method) A separate repository both sites consume, released as versioned files they pin; the sync stops carrying it.
- **Same bytes served** (method) The move is proved by hashing the live reader files before and after.
- **Bugs as passing tests** (method) Record current behaviour; fixing later is a visible change.
- **A two-minute pipeline** (method) Node, three browser engines, a reproducible build, pre-prod, synthetic readers.
- **Reviews and issues** (method) One person and one agent per change; every finding an issue.
- **Go slow to go fast** (claim) The safety net is what lets features keep landing quickly.

> The point is speed. Going slow now is what lets me keep going fast without the fear that each new feature breaks something a reader has paid for. Why the move happens now.

> Same bytes served. How the move is proved.

## [The passkey opens the vault: a door per path, a master vault for every user, and no server of ours](the-passkey-opens-the-vault.md)

2026-10-11 · Vaults & methodSite & engineering

An end-to-end, client-side account with no sign-in to the site: a passkey with the WebAuthn PRF extension gives 32 bytes only the user's authenticator can produce for the site, and because sgit vault keys are made in the client the browser computes a door vault's key and address from them, so nothing is stored or found first; the door holds the master vault's key and a record of its provider, path, credential id, device and date, and the master holds the keys of the vaults below, received read keys, the access key, key pairs generated at random and never derived from the passkey, and the list of its doors. A test on newsroom.sgit.ai on 11 and 12 October 2026 held for the platform path, the derivation and a door on a real server, and showed that the same passkey reached by a phone over QR gives different bytes, so the claim is narrowed to the same kind of path and the unit of the design is a door per path: added in the first week while unlocked with no key typed, bootstrapped by the recovery code where no device has both paths, with an unknown address meaning no door here yet and a door retired by deleting its file, never by destroying its derived address.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example

**18 nodes, 19 edges**

- **Signed in where you already are** (concept) Apple, Google or Microsoft syncs the passkey store; the site is never signed in to, and the vault travels with the store.
- **Passkey with PRF** (concept) 32 bytes only your authenticator produces for this site; the same on every device it syncs to, through the same kind of path.
- **A door per path, computed** (method) Key and address computed from the PRF bytes with HKDF; one file holding the master key and its record: provider, path, credential id, device, date.
- **The master vault** (artefact) The keys of the vaults below, received read keys, the access key, random key pairs, and the list of doors with their keys.
- **Where the key lives: nowhere** (claim) sgit keys are made in the client, so the door is computed, not stored; the lab created one on a real server and opened it again.
- **The recovery code, a door of its own** (method) 128 bits, shown once; derives the recovery door, and is the way a new path joins where no device has both paths.
- **No third-party scripts where keys live** (claim) Storage is per origin; the unlock page loads nothing it did not build.
- **PRF support in 2026** (example) Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello, Firefox; tested on a Mac, an iPhone and an iPad.
- **Accounts with no server** (claim) Any static site: sign in, open your own data on any device, unreadable by the operator.
- **Where the passkey lives** (claim) A synced provider or a hardware key gives every device; a clean browser gives one device plus recovery; Chrome's own store has no PRF.
- **A lock, not an identity** (claim) Key pairs are generated at random and stored in the top, never derived from the passkey, so the identity survives any change of lock.
- **Several passkeys, several masters** (method) A second passkey for another role computes its own doors to its own master; the store's picker is the switch.
- **Retire a door, never destroy its address** (method) A door is retired by deleting its one file; a destroyed vault id can never be used again, and a door's address is derived from the passkey.
- **Vaults all the way down** (concept) The pattern already in use: vaults that hold the keys of other vaults, so a read key to one child exposes nothing above it.
- **The test, 11 and 12 October** (example) One Google Password Manager passkey: the same bytes on a Mac and an iPhone by the platform path; different bytes, consistently, when the phone answered a QR code from an iPad or that Mac.
- **The unit is the path** (claim) Whatever produced a distinct set of bytes gets a distinct door; every door points at the same master.
- **Add a door, no key typed** (method) While unlocked, ask for the bytes by the other path and write the new door from memory; a normal first-week step.
- **No door here yet** (claim) An unknown derived address means a path with no door; the page offers an open device or the recovery code, never an error.

> The same passkey gives the same bytes on every device it syncs to, **through the same kind of path**. The narrowed claim.

> The test is the requirement. Why the door layer is back.

## [I miss it, so it is working: the people who decide the roadmap have to use the product, and the vault the newsroom now needs](i-miss-it.md)

2026-10-11 · Startups & strategySite & engineering

The people who decide a roadmap have to use the product: they give the best feedback and direction, and when they do not use it, something is missing. Dinis failed that test with earlier startups and the vaults now pass it, getting better because they are used. With agents able to build almost anything, direction from usage is the scarce part, and the speed of the loop from comment to article to feature is the moat. Reading the newsroom on four devices that do not agree is the signal for the next feature: the reader's own encrypted vault, with an access key, a key pair, a log per device merged by union, a way to add a device, and a one-way line to the agent that edits the site.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example

**8 nodes, 7 edges**

- **Whether they miss it** (concept) The test applies to the makers as much as the customers.
- **Makers as users** (claim) Developers, product owners and founders use it daily, on real work.
- **Good ideas I did not use** (example) The Cyber Boardroom, MyFeeds and early sgit: the signal I missed.
- **The vaults pass the test** (example) Created all the time by me and my agents; 54 published; better because used.
- **Direction is the scarce part** (claim) Agents can build almost anything; usage supplies direction, context and focus.
- **The loop is the moat** (claim) Comment, article, feature: 81 minutes for the reading list.
- **Four devices, four newsrooms** (example) Separate balances, personas and histories in each browser.
- **The reader's own vault** (method) Access key, key pair, a log per device merged by union, add a device, a line to the agent.

> Momentum does not come from the plan. It comes from use. Why releasing and using matter.

> if I have access, I can customise it, I can do a lot with it, and I still do not use it, then something is missing. The test, applied to the makers.

## [Brief the agent too: the people I talk to work with agents, so what I send has to reach both](brief-the-agent-too.md)

2026-10-11 · Vaults & methodNews & evidence

Readers increasingly read through an agent. A founder gave an article on threat tiers to their agent, which saw the team defending against states while backups were undone and reset the target to T3. So content should travel by several routes: to the person, to their agent as a plain-text brief with the articles by number, reasons, graph slices and rules for critical reading, back from the agent to the person as a translation, and later agent to agent through an encrypted lane. Articles are compression we control, which keeps workflows affordable; an agent with an account and memory should read only the delta, which is what it would pay for. Packs must be written safely: data not instructions, nothing hidden, nothing that acts for us, disagreement invited.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example

**9 nodes, 8 edges**

- **The founder's agent and the threat tiers** (example) Defending against states with no backups; reset to T3 after one article.
- **Routes a message takes** (concept) Me to person, me to their agent, agent to person, me to my agent, agent to agent.
- **The agent as a better reader** (claim) More detail, read against the project, challenged rather than accepted.
- **A pack for someone's agent** (method) Plain text: who, the list by number, reasons, graph slices, rules, where to continue.
- **Memory and the delta** (concept) Read what changed, not everything again; what an agent would pay for.
- **Articles as controlled compression** (claim) Why our workflows stay within budget.
- **Writing to someone else's agent safely** (method) Data not instructions; nothing hidden; nothing that acts for us; disagreement invited.
- **Onboarding by reading** (example) Every new session reads the same sites first; package it for others.
- **What to build next** (artefact) Agent pack on every list, onboarding packs, a changes file, accounts and a direct line.

> Some of what I write is better read by their agent. The shift for a writer.

> A pack that asks for agreement is not worth sending. The rule for writing to someone else's agent.

## [From me to you, in a link: a personal reading list, two briefs to build and use it, and the loop that makes it a day's work](a-reading-list-in-a-link.md)

2026-10-11 · Site & engineeringStartups & strategy

A personal reading list in a URL fragment (from, to, article numbers to read, to look at, and to follow) that opens on the newsroom as a persona the reader can keep or remove, with a stable public number for every article and a page to make a list for anyone. Two briefs: the newsroom builds it with validation, tests and no tracking; the RiskMandate agent, which keeps the contacts, chooses the person with Dinis, researches public sources, picks articles with reasons, tests the link, drafts the email, and Dinis sends it. The core is the loop: editorial, product, engineering, sales and the founder connected by written briefs, small contracts, owned repositories and tests, closing in about a day, as it did this week, with costs that are written down: drift, budgets and one person as the router.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example

**10 nodes, 9 edges**

- **A reading list in a link** (method) Names and article numbers in the fragment; the server never sees them.
- **A number for every article** (concept) Assigned once, never changed or reused: the contract for links.
- **The list becomes a persona** (method) Added as a visitor, kept or removed in one tap.
- **Anyone can make a list** (claim) Curating for someone else becomes a link, and a business model.
- **The RiskMandate agent uses it** (method) Choose, research, pick with reasons, test, draft; Dinis sends.
- **Nothing tracks the reader** (claim) No opens counted; the conversation starts with a reply.
- **The loop** (concept) Five parts of a company connected by written briefs, closing in about a day.
- **This week's loops** (example) Personas by link 17 hours after the brief; three articles corrected 32 minutes after payments went live.
- **What the loop costs** (claim) Drift between parts, session budgets, and one person as the router.
- **Vibe coding with a slow loop** (concept) Product owners always described software; the loop was the bottleneck.

> The loop is fast because those costs are written down, not because they are gone. The honest version of the claim.

> An article number that never changes is a contract. Why two parts can move independently.

## [A model in the tab: Chrome now ships an LLM to capable desktops, and it is the hardest piece of the client-side puzzle](a-model-in-the-tab.md)

2026-10-11 · Site & engineeringGraphs & knowledge

Since Chrome 148 any page can prompt Gemini Nano on the reader's device, which supplies the hardest missing piece of the client-side pattern; the rough first run is mostly fixable by the page, the scarcity of examples has real causes, the standards objections are serious, and the way to build on it without being captured is to keep the meaning in anchored graphs and use the model as a checkable function.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**10 nodes, 10 edges**

- **The Prompt API, stable in Chrome 148** (artefact) Gemini Nano on the device: text, image and audio in, text or JSON out.
- **The last piece of the client-side puzzle** (claim) Intelligence was what kept a back end in the picture.
- **The download never stopped** (example) The page lost the progress bar on refresh; the download carried on.
- **Why there are so few examples** (claim) New, gated hardware, a 4 GB first run, five languages, no native tools, contested.
- **The case against** (concept) Prompts do not travel; a vendor policy in front of a web API; the browser decides the model.
- **Keep the meaning in the data** (method) Anchored graph slices and narrow schema-constrained questions make the model replaceable.
- **Graph answers fit a small window** (claim) A 2,600-token anchored slice fits; the prose does not.
- **A download panel that tells the truth** (method) Bytes, rate, time left, survives a refresh, explains unavailable.
- **Ask this article, personas, voice memos** (example) The first uses: grounded answers, local personas, on-device transcription.
- **What is fast enough, on which machines?** (question) Speed, context window and accuracy are unmeasured; the vault will measure them.

> Keep the meaning in the data, not in the prompt. How to build on one vendor's model without being captured by it.

> The page should be complete without the model, and better with it. The design rule for a gated, contested capability.

## [No server, by design: first I retired the database, now I am retiring the back end](no-server-by-design.md)

2026-10-11 · Site & engineeringVaults & method

After replacing the database with the file system (LETS), the next step is removing the back end: encrypted vaults make the server blind, so the application moves to the browser, leaving only commodity products on the server side; the security gaps this leaves are written down and accepted because they do not match the threat, and the result scales without its complexity scaling and ships as files.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example**question

**10 nodes, 11 edges**

- **The file system is the database** (method) LETS: load, extract, transform, save; every state a file you can version and read.
- **No back end** (claim) All application logic runs in the reader's browser.
- **A blind server** (concept) Vaults are encrypted in the client, so anything that reads data must run where the key is.
- **Commodity servers, not no servers** (claim) Static hosting, a ciphertext store, a payment link, DNS and CI, with a sign-in provider next, all products.
- **The SGit Newsroom** (example) Personas, a reading meter, a payment on-ramp, a newsroom of your own, encrypted sharing, in-browser databases.
- **Gaps written down and accepted** (method) SG Meter's security model: every cheat changes a number only the cheater sees.
- **Scales without complexity scaling** (claim) More readers add bandwidth against cached files, not moving parts.
- **A release is a set of files** (example) 114 releases in eleven days; the meter in seven releases in an afternoon.
- **Sovereignty, privacy, explainability, determinism** (concept) The pattern's properties, not its policies.
- **How far can it be pushed?** (question) Secrets the reader must not hold are the honest boundary.

> Encryption came first, and the client-side architecture followed, because there was nowhere else for the logic to go. The constraint that designed it.

> First the database went, and the work got simpler. Now the back end is going, and the work is getting faster. The pattern in two sentences.

## [The agent is the reader: why agents will pay for graphs, personas and signed claims, because it is cheaper than not paying](the-agent-is-the-reader.md)

2026-10-11 · News & evidenceStartups & strategy

When agents are the readers, a publisher that serves curated meaning, an anchored graph fitted to the agent's persona and objective, and claims signed with an expiry saves the agent more tokens than it charges, so the agent pays not to pay; measured on five articles the graph answers in 90% fewer tokens, and on 70 articles compression with scale appears only where a Cartographer curates, which is the work worth paying for.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**example**question

**10 nodes, 11 edges**

- **The graph is bigger than the text** (example) The full catalogue is 2.8 times the articles; the concept index is 7%.
- **A question costs 90% less in the graph** (claim) Median 2,579 tokens against 25,698, across all 45 concepts, with anchors.
- **Making the map is the verification** (example) 32 flags, 37 corrections, one systematic catch; the cost per finding rises on the third pass.
- **Compression with scale needs curation** (claim) 908 of 928 uncurated labels unique; 114 curated mentions over 45 concepts.
- **Projected to 100,000 articles** (claim) Curated index 150 to 2,660 times smaller; a question about 13,000 tokens; search sees 2%.
- **PageRank with meaning** (concept) Typed edges citing their sentences say what a link means; a two-article loop tops our own PageRank.
- **Agents are personas too** (concept) An agent arrives with an objective; the slice fitted to it is the product.
- **The agent pays not to pay** (claim) A fee below the token saving is rational; about ten questions pay for an article's graph.
- **Signed claims with an expiry** (method) A claim re-checked and signed as of a date, until a date, renewed for a fee.
- **Will agents pay?** (question) The rails exist and the arithmetic works on paper; demand is untested.

> Compression with scale is not a property of graphs. It is a property of curation. The hypothesis, tested.

> A reader that saves money by using it will pay for it, not out of goodwill but because paying is cheaper than not paying. The economic model in one sentence.

## [Where the platform draws the line: Microsoft Execution Containers, the shared responsibility model for agents, and the business logic above it](where-the-platform-draws-the-line.md)

2026-10-11 · Agents & policy

Microsoft Execution Containers and the Agent Control Specification confirm the direction of travel, policy outside the agent, deny by default, observe before enforcing, but like the cloud's shared responsibility model they draw the line where the platform can see, at paths, numeric addresses and tool calls, so the business logic above it, what a label means, whose voice, how many, which customer, and who accepts what is left, has to come from the deployer's behaviour policy, which is what turns the platform's hooks into boundaries.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact**example**question

**8 nodes, 7 edges**

- **Microsoft Execution Containers** (artefact) A versioned JSON policy enforced by the OS: sandbox, process, paths, network, desktop; deny by default.
- **Agent Control Specification** (artefact) Eight interception points, a snapshot of the session, a policy engine and a normalised verdict; hooks, not rules.
- **Permissive, learning, enforcement** (method) Measure the reach, calibrate it, enforce it: the ABP's three verbs as platform modes.
- **Shared responsibility, for agents** (concept) Every platform draws its line at the granularity it can touch.
- **Business logic above the line** (claim) Labels, voice, quantity and customer are business content no platform can supply.
- **Eight scenarios, three designs** (example) Plain: 8 open. ABP: 8 named, 0 bounded. ABP on MXC and ACS: 3 OS boundaries, 4 if the rule is written, 1 accepted.
- **Same code, different owner** (claim) An MXC file or ACS manifest the agent can edit is a setting, not a boundary.
- **The policy writes the rules** (question) Generating MXC JSON and ACS policies from ABP rows: a design, not a product.

> The unit of restriction is the application and the tool. It is not the data, and it is not the business. The line every platform draws.

> The policy names it, proposes the boundaries that shrink it What a behaviour policy does with a risk inside the mandate.

## [The same argument, in our words: Satya Nadella on models as insider risks, translated into the language of RiskMandate](the-same-argument-in-our-words.md)

2026-10-11 · Agents & policy

Nadella's argument and ours are the same argument in two vocabularies: his lost code path is software was the law, his insider is the ultimate insider, his separation of supply from authority is the grant is not the mandate, his controls outside the model are the enforcer test, and his last line is our brakes; the languages differ in unit, a model against one agent in one deployment, and in frame, observation against authority accepted by a named person for a stated interval.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact

**10 nodes, 9 edges**

- **Models as insider risks** (artefact) Nadella's post, paraphrased throughout and quoted once.
- **Software was the law** (concept) Rules the interface enforced by omission are gone when an agent calls the API.
- **The ultimate insider** (concept) A threat need not be malicious; the distance between benign and hostile is a prompt.
- **Every risk is already accepted** (concept) No deny button; the only questions are who holds it and until when.
- **The grant is not the mandate** (concept) Supply arrives with a grant; authority is a mandate with an issuer, scope and clock.
- **The enforcer test** (concept) Only a boundary the agent cannot reach is a control.
- **Reality is the calibrator** (method) Measure the grant on the thing itself and compare the footprint with the mandate.
- **Brakes let a car go fast** (claim) Constraint is what makes autonomy affordable.
- **One agent, one deployment** (claim) Risk is a property of a deployment, not of a model.
- **Authority before observation** (claim) A written mandate and a named acceptor tell you whether what you observed was allowed.

> And a mandate with no clock is just a grant. What authority needs before it is separate from supply.

> Independence is not a property of the checker. It is a property of who controls it. The answer to nested black boxes.

## [Authority outside the model: an answer to Satya Nadella on models as insider risks, principle by principle, with what we run, what we ship and what we plan](authority-outside-the-model.md)

2026-10-11 · Agents & policy

Treating models as insider risks is right, and each of the seven principles maps to something this network runs, publishes or plans, but the principles work only with the column they leave thin: authority written down before the agent runs, a mandate compared with the footprint, risk belonging to one deployment rather than a model, a named owner and expiry for what is left, recoverability beyond the brake, and decisions made in advance as envelopes.

*[diagram]*
**concept**claim**method**artefact

**10 nodes, 9 edges**

- **Models as insider risks** (artefact) Nadella's post: separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it; seven principles.
- **The enforcer test** (concept) A control bounds a grant only if enforced by something the grant does not include.
- **A second reader the agent cannot skip** (method) Code checks first, a different model with less context, fail closed, log every verdict.
- **Same code, different owner** (claim) Whether a check is a setting or a boundary depends on who owns its installation.
- **Evidence the writer cannot edit** (method) Vault history, append lanes, hashed ledgers, the connector twin.
- **The mandate is the missing column** (claim) Observation says what happened; only a written mandate says whether it was allowed.
- **Footprint in the gap is a near miss** (concept) Countable long before anything breaks; the number worth disclosing.
- **Risk belongs to a deployment** (claim) The same model is harmless in one setup and serious in another.
- **A brake does not undo** (claim) Containment needs a list of what can and cannot be reversed.
- **Honest maturity** (artefact) What runs, what is published as design, what is only argued, principle by principle.

> Observation tells you what an agent did. It cannot tell you whether the agent was allowed to, unless somebody wrote down what it was for before it ran. The missing column, in two sentences.

> Containment without recoverability is a brake on a car with no reverse gear. Why the brake is not enough.
